edge_cases.title: A finished thread is still joinable
A data race can delete your loop
The lock that locks nothing
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>{m};` creates a temporary that locks and unlocks immediately, at the end of the full expression.
- `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>(m);` is parsed as a **declaration** of a new default-constructed `unique_lock` named `m`, shadowing the mutex. It locks nothing. GCC warns: "unnecessary parentheses in declaration of 'm'".
- `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(m);` is also a declaration, but `lock_guard` has no default constructor, so it fails to compile (the lucky case).
- `std::scoped_lock lk;` with no arguments compiles and locks nothing.
- Rule: always name the guard: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);`.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Mutexes and Lock Types

edge_cases.title: The notification happened before anyone waited
`x = x + 1` is not `x += 1`
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "`x` is atomic, so any expression on it is atomic."
- What happens: `x = x + 1` calls `load()`, adds in a register, then `store()`. Two threads can both load 5 and both store 6.
- Not undefined behaviour (each access is atomic), but a **logic bug: lost updates**.
- `x += 1`, `++x`, `x.fetch_add(1)` are each one RMW and never lose increments.
```cpp
#include <atomic>
std::atomic<int> x{0};
void bad()  { x = x + 1; }        // load, add, store: can lose updates
void good() { x += 1; }           // one atomic RMW (lock add on x86)
int main() { bad(); good(); return x.load() == 2 ? 0 : 1; }
```
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::atomic and Compare-and-Swap

edge_cases.title: Acquire on one side only gives you nothing
Holder preempted while waiters spin (oversubscription)
edge_cases.explanation:
- With more runnable threads than cores, the holder can be descheduled mid-section.
- Waiters then spin for whole time slices, and they are the very threads stopping the holder from being rescheduled.
- Measured on a 20-CPU machine with 80 threads: a TAS spinlock took 16 to 19 s for work a `std::mutex` did in under 1 s.
- Deep dive: Topic 7, Spinlocks, Busy-Waiting and Backoff

edge_cases.title: A null check does not detect a freed node
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "Before dereferencing `old`, check it is not null."
- What happens: T1 loads `old = A`. T2 pops A and `delete`s it. T1's `old` still holds A's address: `old != nullptr` is true, `old->next` is a use-after-free (UB).
- `delete p` only affects the object, not every copy of the pointer in other threads.
- Fix: a reclamation scheme (hazard pointers, epochs, RCU) or never freeing nodes while the structure is live.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem

edge_cases.title: Full check on masked indices never fires
edge_cases.explanation:
- Assumption: with wrapped indices, "full" is `(tail & mask) + 1 == (head & mask)`.
- Reality: when `tail & mask == N - 1`, the left side is `N`, which can never equal a masked value. The push proceeds, `tail` wraps to equal `head`, and a full queue now looks **empty**: N elements silently disappear.
- Correct options:
  - Monotonic indices: `full = (tail - head == N)`, `empty = (tail == head)`.
  - Wrapped indices: `full = (((tail + 1) & mask) == head)`, capacity is effectively `N - 1`.
```cpp
// Buggy:   (tail & MASK) + 1 == (head & MASK)  -> with N = 4, tail = 3, head = 0: 4 == 0 is false
// Correct: tail - head == N                     (monotonic size_t indices)
```
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers

edge_cases.title: Discarded std::async future runs synchronously
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume `std::async(std::launch::async, f);` fires and forgets.
- The returned temporary `std::future` is destroyed at the end of the statement, and that destructor waits for the task. Code that "launches" tasks in a loop this way executes them one after another.
```cpp
for (auto& item : items)
    std::async(std::launch::async, process, item); // sequential! each waits
```
- Keep the futures (e.g. in a `std::vector<std::future<void>>`) or use a pool. C++20 compilers warn (`[[nodiscard]]`).
- Deep dive: Topic 10, async, future/promise, thread_local and call_once

edge_cases.title: `request_stop()` does not wake a thread blocked in std::condition_variable
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::condition_variable::wait` knows nothing about stop tokens. A `jthread` whose worker sleeps in `cv.wait(lock, pred)` will not wake on `request_stop()`, so the `jthread` destructor's `join()` blocks forever.
- Fixes:
  - `std::condition_variable_any` with the `wait(lock, token, pred)` overload.
  - Or a `std::stop_callback` that sets a flag under the mutex and calls `cv.notify_all()`.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, C++20 Synchronization: latch, barrier, semaphore, jthread

code_examples.title: Classic two-lock deadlock and the scoped_lock fix
code_examples.explanation:
- Shows the bug shape and the fix side by side for a bank transfer.

- Output: `1000 1000` (each direction moves 100000 units, so they cancel).
- Swapping `transfer` for `transfer_broken` makes the program hang intermittently with both threads in `futex_wait`.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Data Races, Race Conditions and Deadlocks

code_examples.title: Snapshot under the lock, slow work outside
code_examples.explanation:
- The report thread used to hold the mutex for the whole report; now it copies under the lock and formats outside.

- Output:

- Timing-based demo: the 10 ms sleep lets the report thread take its snapshot first, so the report shows the pre-fill position.
- Had `slow_format` run under `book_m`, the fill would wait about 40 ms. In production this shows up as normal p50 with ruined p99/p99.9.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Mutexes and Lock Types
additional_code:
fill waited < 5 ms
report: AAPL=100 MSFT=-50

code_examples.title: Worker pool with graceful (draining) shutdown
code_examples.explanation:
- Multiple consumers, `notify_one` per item, `notify_all` for shutdown, work processed outside the lock.

- Output: `processed=1000 sum=333833500` on every run: shutdown drains the queue before workers exit.
- Swap the exit test for `if (stopping_) return false;` and the count becomes nondeterministic.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, Condition Variables and Producer-Consumer Signalling

code_examples.title: Release/acquire publication of non-atomic data
code_examples.explanation:
- The flag is atomic because it is the synchronization mechanism; the payload stays ordinary memory.

- Output is always `7 101.25 ABC`.
- The guarantee covers every write sequenced before the release, including the heap allocation inside `std::string`.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model

code_examples.title: SPSC ring buffer with padding and cached indices
code_examples.explanation:
- Producer and consumer never share a written variable on the same line; each side reloads the other's index only when it has to.

- Output: `in order: true, sum = 500000500000`.
- Runs clean under `-fsanitize=thread`. Removing either `release` (or either `acquire`) makes TSan report a data race on `buf_`.
- `cached_head_` is touched only by the producer and `cached_tail_` only by the consumer, so they are plain variables sitting on their owner's line.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers

code_examples.title: Magic static vs call_once for lazy initialization
code_examples.explanation:
- Both are thread-safe; the static is simpler when the job is "construct one object".

- Output: `Config constructed once` and `Registry loaded once` (either order), then `entries: 3`.
- `once_flag` as a member gives "once per object", which a function-local static (once per program) cannot express.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, async, future/promise, thread_local and call_once

interview_qa.question: Is this code safe?
interview_qa.answer: No. The lambda captures value by reference and the thread is detached, so foo() can return and destroy value before the thread reads it. Reading it then is a dangling reference access: undefined behaviour: depending on timing it may print 42, 0 or garbage.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Two interleavings are possible: the worker reads first (appears to work) or `foo()` returns first (UB). In practice `foo()` often returns before the thread even starts, but timing varies, so a passing test proves nothing.
- Fixes: capture by value `[value]`, or `join()` before returning, or pass owning data (`std::make_shared`) to the detached thread.
- Capturing by value fixes this variable only; any pointer, reference or `this` captured is still a lifetime hazard.
- Also: `std::cout` used by a detached thread while `main` returns and static destruction runs is another hazard.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It is fine because the thread starts immediately." There is no such guarantee.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: tools catch this: AddressSanitizer reports `stack-use-after-return` (with detection enabled), ThreadSanitizer may report races. Code review rule: `detach()` plus `[&]` is almost always a bug.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing
interview_qa.key_takeaway: detach plus reference capture of locals is a dangling reference waiting for the unlucky schedule.
interview_qa.full_content:
```cpp
void foo() {
    int value = 42;
    std::thread t([&] { std::cout << value; });
    t.detach();
}
```

**Answer:**
No. The lambda captures value by reference and the thread is detached, so foo() can return and destroy value before the thread reads it. Reading it then is a dangling reference access: undefined behaviour: depending on timing it may print 42, 0 or garbage.

**Explanation:**
- Two interleavings are possible: the worker reads first (appears to work) or `foo()` returns first (UB). In practice `foo()` often returns before the thread even starts, but timing varies, so a passing test proves nothing.
- Fixes: capture by value `[value]`, or `join()` before returning, or pass owning data (`std::make_shared`) to the detached thread.
- Capturing by value fixes this variable only; any pointer, reference or `this` captured is still a lifetime hazard.
- Also: `std::cout` used by a detached thread while `main` returns and static destruction runs is another hazard.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It is fine because the thread starts immediately." There is no such guarantee.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: tools catch this: AddressSanitizer reports `stack-use-after-return` (with detection enabled), ThreadSanitizer may report races. Code review rule: `detach()` plus `[&]` is almost always a bug.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing

**Key takeaway:** detach plus reference capture of locals is a dangling reference waiting for the unlucky schedule.

interview_qa.question: How many threads would you create for purely CPU-bound tasks on 8 cores, and what does hardware_concurrency() tell you?
interview_qa.answer: Start with about one worker per logical CPU available to the process, then benchmark. hardware_concurrency() is only a hint, usually the online logical CPU count, and may be 0. More threads than CPUs adds context switches and cache pressure, not throughput.
interview_qa.explanation:
- At most N threads can execute simultaneously on N **logical** CPUs. With SMT, 8 logical CPUs may be only 4 physical cores sharing execution units.
- 100 workers on 8 CPUs: the OS time-slices them. Costs: context switches, scheduler overhead, cache and TLB pollution, lock holders preempted, worse tail latency.
- `hardware_concurrency()` on Linux does not account for affinity masks or container CPU quotas. Guard against `0`.
- Leave headroom for other threads (I/O, logging, the OS) if latency matters.
- I/O-bound work: more threads than CPUs can help, since they block.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "100 threads gives more parallelism than 8." Not for CPU-bound work.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "8 threads is always optimal." Memory bandwidth, SMT, contention and other load change the optimum; measure.
- ❌ Imprecise answer: "Context switches cause virtual-to-physical detection." Say: more threads increase cache and TLB pressure and scheduling overhead.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for latency-critical work, pin a small number of threads to isolated cores and avoid oversubscription entirely.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CPU-bound: about one thread per available logical CPU, verified by measurement.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition?
interview_qa.answer: A data race is a C++ memory-model violation (unsynchronized conflicting access) and makes the program undefined. A race condition is a logic bug where correctness depends on timing or interleaving; it can exist in completely data-race-free code.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Data race: a property of individual memory accesses. Detectable by tools like TSan.
- Race condition: a property of the algorithm. Tools usually cannot see it because every access is "legal".
- The two overlap but neither contains the other:
  - Data race and race condition: unprotected `++counter`.
  - Race condition, no data race: `if (stock.load() > 0) stock.fetch_sub(1);` with atomics.
  - Data race, no race condition: two threads both store `true` into a plain `bool done`. Logically harmless, still UB.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A data race is just a type of race condition." A data race can exist where the logic does not depend on order at all, and it is a language-level UB rule, not a logic bug.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "data-race-free" is the minimum bar for a defined program; "race-condition-free" is the bar for a correct one.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Data Races, Race Conditions and Deadlocks
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Data race = undefined program; race condition = wrong program; fix both.

interview_qa.question: You make every member of a class `std::atomic`. Is the class now thread-safe?
interview_qa.answer: Not necessarily. It is data-race-free, but any invariant spanning several members or several steps (check-then-act, read-then-update) can still be broken by interleaving. Such invariants need one critical section, one atomic RMW, or a single owner.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Example: a sequencer with `std::atomic<uint64_t> lastApplied`. Two threads both read 103, both decide 104 is next, both apply 104. Duplicate processing with zero data races.
- Using CAS to claim 104 removes the duplicate, but now `lastApplied == 104` is visible before message 104 has been applied: readers act on half-finished state.
- Better options:
  - One mutex held across check, apply and publish.
  - Funnel all messages to one sequencing thread that owns all the state (single-writer, no locks).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Atomics with acquire/release fix it." Memory ordering controls visibility, not the logic of a multi-step algorithm.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in low-latency systems, single-owner state plus queues is often simpler and faster than sprinkling atomics over shared mutable state.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Data Races, Race Conditions and Deadlocks
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Thread safety is about invariants, not individual variables.

interview_qa.question: Two threads are started in order T1, T2, and both lock the same mutex. Does T1 get it first? Is `std::mutex` fair?
interview_qa.answer: No. Creation order says nothing about scheduling, and `std::mutex` makes no fairness or FIFO promise. Whichever thread reaches the lock first wins, and a newly arriving thread can even beat threads that have been waiting.
interview_qa.explanation:
- On glibc, an unlock wakes one sleeping waiter, but a thread that is already running can grab the lock before the woken thread is scheduled (barging). The woken thread re-competes.
- Unfair locks are faster (no forced hand-off to a sleeping thread), at the cost of possible starvation.
- If order matters, use an ordering mechanism: `join()`, a condition variable with a predicate, a semaphore or latch, or a release/acquire flag.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Waiters are served in arrival order." There is no queue discipline in the standard, and real implementations do not provide one.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a ticket lock gives FIFO fairness if you really need it, at a throughput cost.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Mutexes and Lock Types
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Mutex = exclusion, not ordering and not fairness.

interview_qa.question: Does every `mutex.lock()` call go into the kernel?
interview_qa.answer: No. An uncontended lock and unlock are atomic operations in user space. Only when the mutex is held and the waiter decides to sleep does it make a system call (`futex` wait on Linux), and the unlocker makes a wake call only if waiters exist.
interview_qa.explanation:
- glibc's scheme (implementation detail, not a C++ guarantee):
  - Lock fast path: CAS the lock word 0 → 1. Success: done, no kernel.
  - Contended: set the word to 2 ("locked, maybe waiters") and call `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)`; the thread sleeps.
  - Unlock: atomically set it back to 0; if the old value was 2, call `futex(FUTEX_WAKE, 1)`.
- The lock word lives in the process's memory. The kernel only keeps a wait queue keyed by its address while threads sleep.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A mutex always goes through the kernel, so atomics are always faster." Uncontended, a mutex costs about two atomic RMWs.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The kernel maintains a counter that goes 0, 1, 2." The 0/1/2 states are one library's user-space design; describe it as an example, not as how `std::mutex` works.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "Uncontended, a mutex is user-space atomics; under contention it may block via an OS mechanism such as a futex."
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Mutexes and Lock Types
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Uncontended mutexes never touch the kernel; contended waits may.

interview_qa.question: Tail latency spikes because a reporting thread holds the order-book mutex too long. What do you do?
interview_qa.answer: Shrink the critical section: copy only the needed state under the lock, release it, and build the report from the private snapshot. Better, decouple completely: have the hot path publish snapshots or events to the reporting thread through a queue, so reporting can never block it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Fix lock-induced tail latency by shortening hold time, not by changing the lock type.

interview_qa.question: The producer sets a plain `bool ready` and notifies without locking the mutex. What is wrong?
interview_qa.answer: The write races with the consumer's read of `ready` inside the predicate: a data race, so undefined behaviour. The CV gives no memory ordering for `ready`; the mutex does. It also reopens the lost-wakeup window. Modify `ready` while holding the mutex, then notify.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Two requirements, two tools:
  - mutex: mutual exclusion and happens-before for the shared state;
  - CV: efficient blocking and waking.
- With the mutex: producer `unlock(m)` synchronizes-with the consumer's subsequent `lock(m)`, so everything written before the unlock is visible after the lock.
- `notify_one` is not specified to synchronize your data; never use it as a publication mechanism.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It only risks a lost wakeup." The first problem is undefined behaviour from the data race; the lost wakeup is a second, separate failure.

interview_qa.question: Should you call `notify_one` while holding the mutex or after unlocking it?
interview_qa.answer: Both are correct; what must be under the mutex is the state change, not the notify. Notifying after unlock is usually cheaper because the woken thread can take the mutex at once. Notify under the lock when the waiter might destroy the CV immediately after seeing the new state.

interview_qa.question: After `notify_all`, C1 holds the mutex for 40 s. What do C2 and C3 do, and do they need another notification?
interview_qa.answer: C2 and C3 were already unblocked from the CV; they are now blocked on the mutex, not on the CV. When C1 unlocks, they acquire it one at a time and recheck the predicate. No second notification is needed; if the queue is empty they wait on the CV again.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Notification and mutex acquisition are separate events; keep the locked region tiny.

interview_qa.question: Why does a simple bool stop flag need to be `std::atomic<bool>`?
interview_qa.answer: Because concurrent unsynchronized read and write of a plain bool is a data race, which is undefined behaviour regardless of what the CPU does. The compiler may assume no other thread changes it and hoist the load out of the loop, so the worker can spin forever.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The C++ rule: same memory location, two threads, at least one write, no synchronization, not atomic: **data race, UB**.
- Concrete failure (verified with GCC 11 at `-O2`): `while (running) { ++work; }` is compiled as "read `running` once, then loop forever". The program hangs; at `-O0` it terminates. ThreadSanitizer reports the data race.
- `std::atomic<bool> running{true};` tells the compiler the location is shared: every iteration performs a real atomic load.
- For a pure stop flag that publishes no other data, `relaxed` is enough. Join the worker before destroying what it uses (`join()` provides the synchronization).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "After one or two iterations it will see `false`, so a plain bool is fine." There is no such guarantee; the loop may never re-read it.
- ❌ Another wrong answer: "Use `volatile bool`." `volatile` forces re-reads in practice but is still a data race in C++ and gives no ordering.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: hardware atomicity of a load/store is not the same as C++ synchronization; the language model is what the optimizer reasons about.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::atomic and Compare-and-Swap
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Any variable written by one thread and read by another needs an atomic or a lock, even a bool.

interview_qa.question: Many threads increment one std::atomic<long> metrics counter and it does not scale. Why, and how would you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: Every fetch_add needs exclusive ownership of the same cache line, so the line ping-pongs between cores and operations serialize on line transfers. Fix by removing sharing: per-thread or per-core counters on separate cache lines (alignas(64)), summed on read, or batching local increments.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Scale writes by not sharing them; pad per-thread state to separate cache lines.

interview_qa.question: A colleague says a flag shared by two threads needs `volatile`. Do you agree?
interview_qa.answer: No. `volatile` makes the compiler perform every access, which is meant for memory-mapped I/O and signal handlers, but it gives no atomicity, no data-race freedom and no inter-thread ordering. Concurrent access is still a data race. Use `std::atomic<bool>` (relaxed is fine for a pure stop flag).
interview_qa.explanation:
| | `volatile` | `std::atomic` |
|---|---|---|
| Every access performed | ✅ | ✅ (in effect) |
| Atomic read-modify-write | ❌ | ✅ |
| Data-race free | ❌ | ✅ |
| Release/acquire, happens-before | ❌ | ✅ |
| Typical use | MMIO registers, `sig_atomic_t`, `longjmp` locals | Communication between threads |

- `volatile int n; ++n;` from two threads still loses increments.

- Deep dive: Topic 6, Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model

interview_qa.question: An interviewer says release works by flushing the store buffer. Do you agree?
interview_qa.answer: Not as a definition. C++ release means: if an acquire reads this store's value, everything before the release happens-before everything after that acquire. How it is achieved is the compiler's and CPU's choice. MESI is the hardware mechanism that keeps cache lines coherent; it is related but is not the guarantee.
interview_qa.explanation:
- On x86 a release store is a plain `mov` with no flush at all; TSO already keeps stores in order. On ARMv8 it is `stlr`. Neither is "flush the store buffer".
- Coherence (MESI) alone does not give ordering: a core can still delay its own stores in a store buffer or process invalidations late, which is why fences and ordered instructions exist.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "release flushes the store buffer; acquire invalidates stale cache and registers".
- ❌ Overcorrection to avoid: "MESI is completely unrelated". Coherence is part of how hardware implements atomicity and visibility.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: answer in three layers. C++: synchronizes-with and happens-before. Compiler: forbids moving earlier accesses below the store and emits the right instruction. Hardware: store buffers, coherence protocol, barriers. Go to the hardware layer only if asked.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Define release/acquire with happens-before; treat store buffers and MESI as implementation details.

interview_qa.question: "Spinlocks are faster than mutexes." Do you agree?
interview_qa.answer: Only in a narrow case: very short critical sections, low contention, and threads pinned to dedicated cores. Then spinning skips a microseconds-long sleep/wake. With long holds or more runnable threads than cores, spinlocks waste CPU and can be many times slower.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Sleep/wake cost: syscall, context switch, scheduler latency, cache pollution; typically a few microseconds or more.
- Spinning cost: a whole core for the duration of the wait.
- Measured on a 20-CPU machine, tiny section:
  - 8 threads: TTAS spinlock ≈ 0.6 to 0.8 s, `std::mutex` ≈ 0.85 to 0.95 s;
  - 80 threads: TAS spinlock ≈ 16 to 19 s, `std::mutex` ≈ 0.9 s.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Low-latency systems always use spinlocks." They spin where cores are dedicated and sections are tiny, but first try to remove sharing entirely.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "A spinlock can win when the expected wait is shorter than a context switch and the holder is guaranteed to be running; otherwise blocking is better."
- Deep dive: Topic 7, Spinlocks, Busy-Waiting and Backoff
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Spinning is a bet that the lock frees up before a sleep would have paid off.

interview_qa.question: What happens at the hardware level when 32 threads spin on `exchange`, and how does test-and-test-and-set help?
interview_qa.answer: Each `exchange` is a write, so every waiter keeps demanding exclusive ownership of the lock's cache line, bouncing it between cores and delaying the holder's unlock. TTAS spins on a plain load, which keeps a shared copy locally, and only tries the RMW when the lock looks free.
interview_qa.explanation:
- TAS loop: RMW, RMW, RMW... Each one invalidates the other cores' copies; the line ping-pongs.
- TTAS loop:

```cpp
while (true) {
    if (!locked.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) break;  // try
    while (locked.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) cpu_relax();    // test, local
}
```

- While the lock is held, TTAS waiters generate no coherence traffic. On release there is one invalidation and a burst of RMWs, one of which wins.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Waiters are just reading the value until it changes." In the TAS loop they are writing; that is the whole problem.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: TTAS still has a thundering-herd burst on every release; backoff, ticket locks, or MCS queue locks (each waiter spins on its own line) scale further.
- Deep dive: Topic 7, Spinlocks, Busy-Waiting and Backoff

// 32 threads wait on:
while (locked.exchange(true)) {}

interview_qa.question: My code uses only std::atomic and no mutex. Is it lock-free?
interview_qa.answer: Not necessarily. If a thread can wait on a condition another thread must clear (a spinlock built from atomic_flag, a "busy" flag), it is blocking. It also needs every atomic it uses to be lock-free and every call on the path (such as the allocator) to be non-blocking.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `while (flag.test_and_set()) {}` is a lock: if the holder is preempted, all other threads spin without progress. That is blocking.
- `std::atomic<T>` with a large `T` uses an internal lock (check `is_always_lock_free`); a 16-byte tagged pointer is reported not lock-free by GCC.
- `new` / `malloc` in a push can take allocator locks.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "No `std::mutex`, therefore lock-free." Locks can be hand-rolled from atomics, and hidden in library calls.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: lock-freedom is a property of the whole operation path; the typical proof is "every failed CAS implies another thread's CAS succeeded, and no step waits on another thread's state".
- Deep dive: Topic 8, Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Lock-free is about who can stall whom, not which headers you include.

interview_qa.question: What is the ABA problem? Walk through a concrete interleaving.
interview_qa.answer: CAS checks only that a value equals what you read, not that it never changed. If it goes A to B and back to A, CAS succeeds although the state your update depended on is gone. In a stack pop, T1 reads head A and next B, sleeps; others pop A, pop B, push A; T1's CAS installs stale B.
interview_qa.explanation:
```text
stack: head -> A -> B -> C
T1: old = A, next = B         (preempted)
T2: pop A, pop B (free B), push A     -> head -> A -> C
T1: CAS(head, A, B) succeeds          -> head -> B (freed), A is lost
```
- The name: the value went A, then B, then A again.
- The bug is not the CAS itself; it is the **cached `next`**, computed from a state that no longer exists.
- Where the recycled A comes from: the same node pushed back (pools/free lists) or `malloc` returning the freed address for a new node.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "CAS guarantees nothing changed since I read it." It guarantees only equality at the moment of the CAS.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: ABA matters when the CAS value **stands for** more state (a pointer with a `next` behind it). For a plain counter, A to B to A is harmless.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CAS compares values, not histories; pointers recycle.

interview_qa.question: Is a lock-free data structure faster than a mutex-protected one?
interview_qa.answer: Not necessarily. Both serialize on the same hot cache line, lock-free adds failed-CAS retries and reclamation overhead, and an uncontended mutex is just two atomic RMWs. Lock-free wins on progress (no stalling behind a preempted holder) and often tail latency, not raw throughput.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured (4 threads, push/pop on one stack): both versions about 20x slower than single-threaded; lock-free modestly faster, not dramatically.
- Where lock-free loses or ties:
  - high contention on one word (retry storms),
  - per-node allocation (`new` may lock) and reclamation fences,
  - more CASes per operation than a mutex's lock + unlock.
- Where it wins:
  - oversubscription: a mutex holder preempted mid-critical-section stalls everyone,
  - real-time/priority constraints, signal handlers,
  - predictable worst-case progress.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Lock-free is always faster because there is no kernel call." Uncontended mutexes do not enter the kernel either.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the bigger win is usually removing sharing (sharded data, SPSC queues per pair). Decide by requirements, then measure p50 and p99.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Choose lock-free for its progress guarantee, not on an assumption of speed.

interview_qa.question: Why is the capacity of a ring buffer usually a power of two? Is `%` really that slow?
interview_qa.answer: With a power of two, `i % N` equals `i & (N - 1)` for unsigned `i`, a single AND instead of a division. For a compile-time constant N the compiler already does this for unsigned types; the mask matters when N is a runtime value or the index is signed.
interview_qa.explanation:
- A 64-bit integer division costs tens of cycles on many CPUs; an AND costs one.
- `static_assert((N & (N - 1)) == 0)`: with N = 6, `i & 5` maps 0..7 to 0,1,0,1,4,5,4,5, so slots collide and others are never used.
- Power-of-two N also keeps monotonic `size_t` indices consistent across 2^64 wraparound.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Masking is required for correctness." Correctness needs either mask-with-power-of-two or a true modulo; the power of two buys speed and wrap safety.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a power-of-two size may waste memory (need 1100 slots, get 2048); some designs accept a non-power-of-two size with a conditional reset (`if (++i == N) i = 0;`), which is also cheap and branch-predictable.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Power of two makes wrapping a mask; only mask if N really is a power of two.

interview_qa.question: Your market-data SPSC ring is full and the feed handler has another message. What do you do?
interview_qa.answer: It depends on the data semantics. Blocking stalls the feed handler (and the socket), dropping or overwriting creates a sequence gap that corrupts an incremental book. For incremental data: never drop silently; flag overflow, alarm, and resynchronise from a snapshot; fix the slow consumer.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Options and costs:
  - Block or spin: backpressure moves upstream; the kernel socket buffer fills and the NIC/kernel starts dropping UDP packets instead.
  - Drop newest / fail push: lose the incoming message, count it, raise a gap.
  - Overwrite oldest: lose an **unprocessed** message; also needs two writers of `head` in a lock-free SPSC, which is a race.
  - Conflate per instrument: only valid if messages are full snapshots (latest value wins).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Overwrite the oldest so the consumer gets the latest first." The consumer still reads in order; you silently destroyed a message it had not processed.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: answering with UDP gap recovery. That handles **network** loss. Internal queue overflow is a capacity problem in your own pipeline; recovery only cleans up after it.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the ring absorbs bursts; persistent fullness means the consumer's sustained rate is too low, so profile and optimise the consumer (allocations, cache misses, syscalls, page faults, contention, core isolation) or split the work.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers

interview_qa.question: Why not simply make the ring buffer huge so it never fills?
interview_qa.answer: A larger queue only postpones overflow under sustained overload and converts it into latency: messages are still valid but stale by the time they are processed. It also increases memory and cache footprint. Size for legitimate bursts and monitor depth.
interview_qa.explanation:
- If sustained arrival > service, any finite queue fills; size only changes when.
- Depth is delay: 90k queued at 20k/s means trading on prices 4.5 s old.
- "Valid but stale": the messages are correct records of the past, just not useful for a decision now.
- A huge ring also hurts locality (the working set no longer fits in L2/L3) and can hide overload from monitoring.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The data is all valid, so a bigger buffer is pure upside."
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The fix is to slow down the producer." You cannot throttle an exchange feed; the consumer must keep up (consumer capacity ≥ arrival rate).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: export queue depth, high-water mark and estimated queueing delay as metrics, alarm on them, and benchmark p99/p99.9 end-to-end latency.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers

interview_qa.question: Would you use std::async inside a low-latency hot path, for example once per incoming market data message?
interview_qa.answer: No. With libstdc++ each launch::async call creates a thread (tens of microseconds), allocates a shared state, and depends on OS scheduling, so latency is high and unpredictable. Hot paths use preallocated queues feeding long-lived, pinned worker threads.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Per call costs: thread creation (`clone`, stack mapping), heap allocation of the shared state, context switches, cache misses on a cold thread, plus the blocking-destructor behaviour.
- `std::async` gives no control over core affinity, priority, queue bounds, or allocation.
- Even a thread-pool implementation (MSVC) still allocates and has unknown scheduling.
- Low-latency pattern: market data thread pushes into a preallocated SPSC ring buffer, consumed by a processing thread pinned to an isolated core, with no allocation per message.
- Capturing `[&]` the message in an async task that outlives the callback is also a lifetime bug.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "async is cheap because the library optimizes it." The standard gives no performance guarantees, and mainstream Linux implementations spawn a thread per call.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `std::async` is fine for coarse-grained, occasional work (startup, batch jobs) where microseconds do not matter.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, async, future/promise, thread_local and call_once
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Convenient is not cheap: keep std::async off any path measured in microseconds.

interview_qa.question: Why is this lazy-init check broken with threads, and does making `initialized` a `std::atomic<bool>` fix it?
interview_qa.answer: With a plain bool it is a data race, undefined behaviour, and two threads can both see false and both run init(). An atomic<bool> removes the UB but not the double init: the check and the set are separate steps. Use std::call_once or a function-local static.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Interleaving: T1 reads false, T2 reads false, both call `init()`, both set true.
- Even when `init()` runs once, other threads that see `initialized == true` may not see the data `init()` wrote unless the flag uses release/acquire (plain bool gives no ordering at all).
- `std::call_once` provides: election of one executor, blocking of the others until it finishes, publication of its writes to all returning callers, retry on exception.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`call_once` is just a wrapper around these three lines." The three lines have none of these guarantees.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "atomic<bool> fixes it." Atomic steps do not make an atomic sequence.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a CAS on an atomic state (0 = uninit, 1 = running, 2 = done) can elect one initializer, but losers must then wait for state 2, which is reimplementing `call_once`.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, async, future/promise, thread_local and call_once
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Once-only initialization needs election + waiting + publication; that is what call_once is.

```cpp
    init();
    initialized = true;
}
```

interview_qa.question: How does std::counting_semaphore differ from std::mutex? Could binary_semaphore replace a mutex?
interview_qa.answer: A semaphore is a counter of permits with no owner: any thread may `release()`, even one that never acquired. A mutex has an owner that must unlock it. A binary semaphore can provide exclusion, but you lose ownership checks, so it is meant for signalling, not as a mutex replacement.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `counting_semaphore<K> s{init}`: `acquire()` blocks while the count is 0, then decrements; `release(n)` increments and wakes waiters.
- Use cases: limit concurrency to K (connection pools, in-flight requests), count available items, cross-thread signalling (`binary_semaphore` initialised to 0).
- Mutex-only properties a semaphore lacks: owner thread, unlock-by-owner rule, `lock()`/`unlock()` so `std::lock_guard`/`std::scoped_lock` work, recursive variants, potential priority inheritance on some platforms.
- `std::lock_guard<std::binary_semaphore>` does not even compile: there are no `lock`/`unlock` members.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A binary semaphore is just a faster mutex." Semantics differ: a stray `release()` from another thread silently "unlocks" it; releasing past `max()` is undefined behaviour.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the initial count is a design decision: `{0}` means "signal not yet given", `{K}` means "K permits free". Getting it wrong lets a consumer pass before data exists.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, C++20 Synchronization: latch, barrier, semaphore, jthread
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Semaphore = permits without ownership (signalling, throttling); mutex = ownership (exclusion).

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error.
libstdc++: static assertion failed: std::thread arguments must be invocable after conversion to rvalues
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::thread` stores a copy of `value` and passes it to the lambda as an **rvalue**.
- An rvalue cannot bind to a non-const `int&`, so the callable is not invocable with the stored arguments.
- It does **not** silently bind the reference to the hidden copy, and nothing dangles: it just fails to compile.
- With `std::ref(value)` the program prints `43` then `43`.
- **Key Concept:** Reference parameters require std::ref; std::thread never preserves references implicitly.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: ptr points to a destroyed object. Often prints 42 or garbage.
```

**Explanation:**
- `value` lives on the worker's stack and is destroyed when `worker()` **returns**, before `join()` returns.
- The write to `ptr` is properly synchronized (thread completion synchronizes-with `join()`), so there is no data race on `ptr` itself.
- But the object it points to is dead. `join()` does not extend the worker's locals.
- **Key Concept:** Synchronization and object lifetime are separate questions; both must be satisfied.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

int main() {
    int result = 0;                              // owned by main
    std::thread t([&result] { result = 42; });   // main outlives the use
    t.join();                                    // write is visible after join
    std::cout << result << '\n';
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer: Data race (undefined behaviour). In practice it prints 2, not 200000.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Without braces, the loop body is only the declaration `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx);`. The guard locks and immediately unlocks 100000 times, protecting nothing.
- `++counter` runs once per thread, after the loop, with no lock held. The two increments race.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.answer: Undefined behaviour: the same std::mutex is passed twice. Observed with libstdc++: prints "start" and then spins at 100% CPU forever ("done" is never printed).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `scoped_lock` calls `std::lock(m, m)`. The implementation locks `m`, then calls `try_lock` on `m`, which the thread already owns. For a non-recursive mutex that call is UB.
- In libstdc++ the `try_lock` simply fails, so `std::lock` unlocks and retries in an endless loop: a single-thread livelock.
- Deadlock avoidance only works for distinct mutexes. Aliasing (`from == to`) is common in real code: self-transfers, swapping an object with itself, merging a container into itself.
- **Key Concept:** Always handle aliasing before multi-locking.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Data Races, Race Conditions and Deadlocks

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.answer: Yes, it always deadlocks. Prints "main: joining" and then hangs forever.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `main` owns `m` and then waits in `join()` for the worker to finish.
- The worker cannot finish: it is blocked in `lock()` on `m`, which `main` never releases because `g` lives until the end of `main`.
- Circular wait with one mutex: the second resource is "worker has finished".
- Rule: never block waiting for another thread (`join`, `future::get`, a full queue) while holding a lock that thread might need.
- **Key Concept:** A deadlock needs a cycle of waits, not two mutexes.

- `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>(mtx);` is parsed as a declaration: a new default-constructed `unique_lock` named `mtx`, which shadows the global mutex inside the loop body. A default-constructed `unique_lock` owns nothing.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.answer: Yes, always (even single-threaded). Prints "reader: key missing, upgrading" and then hangs: undefined behaviour, self-deadlock.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The exclusive lock must wait until all shared owners release. The thread itself is a shared owner and is now blocked, so it waits for itself forever.
- `std::shared_mutex` offers no upgrade. Even if it did, two readers upgrading at the same time would deadlock each other.
- Correct pattern: drop the shared lock, take the exclusive lock, re-check (another writer may have inserted the key in the gap).
- **Key Concept:** Shared to exclusive is release-then-acquire-then-recheck, never an in-place upgrade.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
timeout ready=1
```

**Explanation:**
- `notify_one` ran when nobody was waiting, so it was dropped. CVs do not remember notifications.
- The raw `wait_for` therefore blocks for the full 200 ms and reports `timeout`, although `ready` has been `true` the whole time.
- With a plain `cv.wait(lk)` this program would hang forever.
- (A spurious wakeup could in theory print `no_timeout`; that would not mean anything was signalled either.)
- `cv.wait_for(lk, 200ms, [] { return ready; })` returns `true` immediately without blocking.
- **Key Concept:** Wait for the state, not for the notification.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, Condition Variables and Producer-Consumer Signalling

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
returned, predicate calls=1, owns lock=1
```

**Explanation:**
- `wait(lk, pred)` is `while (!pred()) wait(lk);`. The predicate is evaluated once, before any blocking.
- It is already `true`, so the thread never blocks and no notification is needed.
- The lock is still owned on return (it was never released).
- This is exactly why "notify before wait" is harmless with the predicate form.
- **Key Concept:** The predicate is checked first; a CV wait on an already-true condition costs one function call.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, Condition Variables and Producer-Consumer Signalling

practice_tasks.answer: No data race, but updates can be lost: any multiple of 4 from 8 to 8000. Run-dependent (eight test runs printed 8000, 4368, 6320, 8000, 7516, 8000, 7584, 8000).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `counter = counter + 4` is `operator int()` (atomic load), an addition in a register, then `operator=` (atomic store).
- Two threads can both load 40 and both store 44: one increment of 4 is lost.
- Because each half is atomic, there is no UB; the bug is a lost update (race condition).
- With only 1000 iterations one thread may finish before the other starts, so 8000 appears in some runs. A passing run proves nothing about correctness.
- `counter += 4` is a single atomic RMW and always gives 8000.
- **Key Concept:** `x += 4` is atomic; `x = x + 4` is load plus store.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::atomic and Compare-and-Swap

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
failed: value=15 expected=15
retry success: value=20 expected=15
```

**Explanation:**
- First CAS: `15 != 10`, so it fails. The atomic is unchanged (15), and `expected` is overwritten with the current value (15).
- Second CAS: `expected` is now 15, which matches, so `value` becomes 20. On success `expected` is not modified.
- This automatic refresh of `expected` is exactly what makes CAS retry loops work without an extra `load()`.
- **Key Concept:** CAS failure writes the current value into `expected`.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::atomic and Compare-and-Swap

practice_tasks.title: Question 13
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
true true false
```

**Explanation:**
- Pointers and 8-byte trivially copyable structs fit a native 8-byte atomic instruction: lock-free.
- A 24-byte struct cannot be updated by one instruction, so `std::atomic<Large>` is implemented with a lock (in GCC's `libatomic`). It is still fully atomic, just not lock-free.
- Doing actual operations on `std::atomic<Large>` with GCC requires linking `-latomic`.
- Platform-specific: the standard only guarantees `std::atomic_flag` is lock-free.
- A "lock-free" algorithm built on `std::atomic<Large>` would silently contain a lock.
- **Key Concept:** `std::atomic<T>` does not imply lock-free; check `is_always_lock_free`.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::atomic and Compare-and-Swap

practice_tasks.title: Question 14
practice_tasks.answer: No. Data race on `payload`: undefined behaviour.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- An acquire load synchronizes-with a **release** store (or a release fence) whose value it reads. A relaxed store has no release semantics.
- So there is still no happens-before from `payload = 500` to the read: the half-fix changes nothing formally.
- "The producer probably runs first" is irrelevant: execution order is not synchronization.
- **Key Concept:** release/acquire is a pair on the same atomic; fixing only the consumer side is the classic half-fix.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model

practice_tasks.title: Question 15
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Possible:   "0 20", "10 20", "20 20"
Impossible: "20 10", "10 0"
(Full allowed set: 0 0, 0 10, 0 20, 10 10, 10 20, 20 20)
```

**Explanation:**
- The modification order of `x` is `0 → 10 → 20` (both stores are in one thread, so sequenced-before fixes their order).
- Read-read coherence: once the reader has observed a value, a later load of the same object cannot return an earlier value in the modification order. This holds even for `relaxed`.
- Reading `a` and `b` in `main` after `join()` is safe: join provides happens-before.
- **Key Concept:** per object, observations never go backward; relaxed only relaxes ordering across different objects.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model

practice_tasks.title: Question 16
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
With seq_cst: "T1", "T2" or "T1 T2". The empty line is impossible.
With release stores / acquire loads: all four, including the empty line.
```

**Explanation:**
- Empty output means both loads read `false`. Then T1's `y.load` precedes T2's `y.store` and T2's `x.load` precedes T1's `x.store` in the single seq_cst total order. With program order that forms a cycle, so it cannot happen.
- "T1 T2" is possible: total order `x.store, y.store, y.load, x.load`.
- Two common wrong answers: "at most one thread can print" (backwards) and "seq_cst allows every outcome" (misses the cycle).
- With release/acquire the store can be delayed past the later load (store buffer), and the empty line really occurs on x86 (thousands of times per 200,000 trials, see Theory Example 3).
- **Key Concept:** store-then-load across two variables (Dekker pattern) needs seq_cst; acquire/release does not forbid it.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model

practice_tasks.title: Question 17
practice_tasks.answer: Data race: undefined behaviour. With g++ 11 -O2 it prints "waiter sees data=0" immediately; other compilers or flags may instead spin forever.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `locked` and `data` are shared without atomics or locks: a data race, so the optimizer may assume no other thread modifies them.
- The loop body has no side effects, and C++ lets the compiler assume such a loop terminates (forward-progress rule). GCC 11 at `-O2` deletes the loop completely: `waiter` prints at once, long before `main` writes `42`.
- Another legal outcome: load `locked` once and turn the loop into `for (;;) {}`, a hang. Both are "correct" compilations of a racy program.
- `volatile bool` would force a reload each iteration but still gives no ordering for `data` and no atomic RMW for building a real lock: still a data race.
- **Key Concept:** Any flag shared between threads must be `std::atomic` (or protected by a lock); with release/acquire it also publishes the data written before it.
- Deep dive: Topic 7, Spinlocks, Busy-Waiting and Backoff

practice_tasks.title: Question 18
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
16 false true
```

**Explanation:**
- `{pointer, 64-bit tag}` is 16 bytes. The CPU has `cmpxchg16b`, but GCC routes 16-byte atomics through `libatomic`, reports them as not always lock-free, and requires `-latomic` to link any operation on them.
- A Treiber stack built on `std::atomic<TaggedPtr>` therefore may contain a hidden lock: not lock-free, even though the source has no mutex.
- Alternatives that fit in one lock-free 8-byte word: a 32-bit node index plus a 32-bit tag (preallocated pool), or a tag in the unused upper bits of a 48-bit x86-64 pointer (narrower, can wrap).
- Clang may inline `cmpxchg16b` with `-mcx16`; results are compiler and flag dependent, so assert it: `static_assert(std::atomic<Head>::is_always_lock_free);`.
- **Key Concept:** Verify the lock-freedom of the atomics your algorithm depends on.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem

practice_tasks.title: Question 19
practice_tasks.answer: accepted=4 empty=true
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `full()` is checked with `tail` at 0, 1, 2, 3. At `tail == 3`, `(3) + 1 == 0` compares `4 == 0`: false, so the 4th push is accepted.
- `tail` becomes 4, `4 & MASK == 0 == head & MASK`, so the queue that holds 4 items now reports **empty**. The consumer would never read them.
- The masked left side can reach `N`, which no masked value ever equals; the test can never fire at the wrap point.
- **Key Concept:** Use monotonic indices (`full = tail - head == N`) or wrapped indices with one sacrificed slot (`full = ((tail + 1) & MASK) == head`).
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers

practice_tasks.title: Question 20
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Packed   16
HeadOnly 64
Both     128
```

**Explanation:**
- `Packed`: both 8-byte atomics share one cache line.
- `HeadOnly`: the struct is 64-byte aligned and padded to 64, but `tail` sits at offset 8, on the **same** line as `head`. Still false sharing.
- `Both`: `tail` starts at offset 64, a different line. Only this layout separates the producer-written and consumer-written indices.
- None of these layouts changes synchronization; the atomics and memory orders do that.
- **Key Concept:** `alignas` aligns the start of one member; give every independently written hot variable its own line.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers

practice_tasks.title: Question 21
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
100 100 100
0
```

**Explanation:**
- Each thread has its own `counter`, starting at 0, incremented 100 times by that thread only.
- No data race: no instance of `counter` is touched by two threads. `result[i]` slots are distinct objects, read after `join()`.
- `main`'s own instance was never incremented.
- **Key Concept:** thread_local means one instance per thread, not one shared variable.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, async, future/promise, thread_local and call_once

practice_tasks.answer:
start

(GCC also warns: ignoring return value of 'std::async', declared with attribute 'nodiscard'.)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::async` returns a temporary `std::future`. It is destroyed at the end of the full expression.
- The last future of an async-launched task **blocks in its destructor** until the task completes.
- So the "background" task runs to completion before `after async` is printed. Deterministic.
- **Key Concept:** A discarded std::async future makes the call synchronous.

```
future_error: std::future_error: Broken promise
true
```

**Explanation:**
- The promise was moved into the lambda, so it is destroyed with the thread's callable after the early `return`.

- `get()` wakes up and throws. No hang.
- The `what()` text is libstdc++'s; the error code is portable.
- **Key Concept:** An abandoned promise breaks loudly instead of leaving waiters stuck.

practice_tasks.title: Question 24
practice_tasks.answer:
Round 1 is correct ("round 1: 21"). From round 2 on: undefined behaviour (count_down() on a latch
already at 0, data race on results). Observed with GCC 11: "round 1: 21", "round 2: 21" (stale), then a hang.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- A latch is one-shot. After round 1 the counter is 0 and stays 0.
- Round 2: `done.wait()` returns immediately, so main reads `results` while the workers may still be writing them: data race (TSan reports it); the printed sums may be stale.
- Each worker's `count_down()` now violates the precondition `update <= counter`: undefined behaviour. libstdc++ simply drives the counter negative; a later `wait()` then waits for a 0 that never comes, which is why the observed run hangs in round 3.
- **Key Concept:** Latches cannot be reset: create one per round, or use `std::barrier` for repeated phases.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, C++20 Synchronization: latch, barrier, semaphore, jthread

practice_tasks.title: Question 25
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
leaving scope
worker: stop seen
after scope
```

**Explanation:**
- At the closing brace `~jthread` runs: `request_stop()`, then `join()`.
- The worker notices `stop_requested()` within about 1 ms, prints, and returns; only then does `join()` return and `main` prints "after scope".
- `jthread` passes its own stop token because the lambda's first parameter is a `std::stop_token`.
- With `std::thread` (and a lambda without the token parameter) the destructor of a joinable thread calls `std::terminate`: the program aborts right after "leaving scope".
- **Key Concept:** `jthread` = request stop + join in the destructor; cancellation is cooperative (the loop must check the token).
- Deep dive: Topic 11, C++20 Synchronization: latch, barrier, semaphore, jthread

quick_reference.content:
#### std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Destroy without join/detach? | `std::terminate()`, because the object is still joinable, even if the thread already finished. |
| What does `joinable()` mean? | Handle owns a thread not yet joined or detached; not "is running". |
| Ways to become non-joinable? | `join()`, `detach()`, moved-from (or default-constructed). |
| Why move-only? | Unique ownership of an OS thread: one owner joins it. |
| How are args passed? | Decay-copied into thread storage in the creating thread, passed as rvalues. |
| `int&` param with plain arg? | Compile error; use `std::ref`. |
| Exception escapes thread? | `std::terminate()`; propagate with `exception_ptr` or futures. |
| What does `join()` guarantee? | Thread finished and its writes happen-before code after `join()`. |
| Does `join()` extend worker locals? | No; they die when the worker function returns. |
| `jthread` destructor? | `request_stop()` then `join()`. |
| `request_stop()` kills the thread? | No, cooperative; worker must check its token. |
| How many threads for CPU-bound work? | Start near available logical CPUs, then benchmark. |
| Thread per task at 10k tasks/s? | No: tens of microseconds per creation; use a pool. |

#### Data Races, Race Conditions and Deadlocks
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Two threads `++x` on plain int? | Data race, undefined behaviour; no value is guaranteed |
| Is `++x` atomic on x86? | No; without `lock` it is a load, add, store |
| Does `join()` fix it? | No; it orders the thread before the joiner, not the threads against each other |
| Race condition without data race? | Yes: atomic check-then-act, or lock-protected but order-dependent logic |
| Data-race-free means deterministic? | No |
| Deadlock conditions? | Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait |
| Cheapest prevention? | Consistent global lock order |
| Locking 2 mutexes in modern C++? | `std::scoped_lock(m1, m2)` |
| Does `lock_guard` detect deadlock? | No |
| Does `try_lock` wait? | No; use `try_lock_for` on a timed mutex |
| Can TSan find deadlocks? | It reports lock-order inversions; use gdb for a live hang |

#### Mutexes and Lock Types
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How does a mutex prevent a data race? | Mutual exclusion plus unlock-synchronizes-with-lock, if every access uses the same mutex |
| Does a mutex decide who goes first? | No |
| `lock_guard` vs `unique_lock`? | Same exclusivity; `unique_lock` adds defer, unlock/relock, move, timed, CV support |
| Why does CV need `unique_lock`? | `wait` must unlock while sleeping and relock before returning |
| Can another thread unlock my mutex? | No, UB; use a semaphore for signaling |
| Thread exits holding the lock? | Lock is never released |
| Does every lock enter the kernel? | No; only contended waits that sleep (and the matching wake) |
| Uncontended cost? | Tens of cycles: a couple of atomic RMWs |
| Is `shared_mutex` faster? | Only for long reads and rare writes; fairness is implementation-defined |
| Shared to exclusive upgrade? | Not supported; release, lock exclusively, re-check |
| Fix a lock held across slow work? | Snapshot under the lock, work outside |
| Global map mutex too hot? | Shard by key; better, single owner per shard |

#### Condition Variables and Producer-Consumer Signalling
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| What is a CV? | A way to block until shared state may have changed; the predicate is the state, the CV is only the doorbell. |
| Why a mutex? | It protects the predicate and lets `wait` release-and-register atomically, closing the lost-wakeup gap. |
| Why `unique_lock`? | `wait` must unlock while blocked and relock before returning; `lock_guard` cannot. |
| Why a loop / predicate? | Spurious wakeups, stolen wakeups, and notifications meant for other predicates. |
| Lost wakeup? | A notify that happens between "checked the state" and "started waiting"; it is dropped because CVs keep no memory. |
| Notify under lock? | Correct either way; after unlock is usually cheaper. |
| `notify_all` cost? | Thundering herd: all wake, serialize on the mutex, most go back to sleep. |
| `wait_for`? | Blocking wait with a deadline; use the predicate overload; timeout is not "condition false". |
| Shutdown? | Predicate `!q.empty() || stopping`, set `stopping` under the lock, `notify_all`, drain or abandon on purpose. |
| Atomic flag without lock? | No data race, but lost wakeup returns; lock the mutex between the store and the notify. |
| CV vs semaphore? | A semaphore remembers releases as a count; a CV forgets notifications. |

#### std::atomic and Compare-and-Swap
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| What does `std::atomic` guarantee? | Indivisible operations on one object, no data race, one modification order; ordering is a separate knob. |
| Is `++atomic` atomic? | Yes, it is an atomic RMW; `x = x + 1` is not. |
| Why does `load`/`store` increment fail? | The gap between two atomic operations, not the local variable. |
| What does CAS do on failure? | Returns false and writes the current value into `expected`. |
| weak vs strong? | Weak may fail spuriously; use it in loops. Strong for one-shot decisions. |
| Why the CAS loop? | Competing writers plus spurious failure; recompute `desired` each time. |
| Is a CAS loop wait-free? | No, lock-free: someone succeeds, a given thread may starve. |
| Is `std::atomic<T>` lock-free? | Not guaranteed; check `is_always_lock_free`; only `atomic_flag` is guaranteed. |
| Does atomic flush the store buffer? | Not a C++ concept; hardware mechanism varies by order and CPU. |
| Atomic or mutex? | Atomic for one independent value, mutex for multi-variable invariants; measure. |
| Can relaxed tear? | No; memory order never affects atomicity. |
| Why atomic for a bool flag? | Plain concurrent access is a data race (UB); compiler may hoist the load. |
| Why do atomics scale badly? | Every write needs exclusive cache-line ownership; the line ping-pongs. |
| `atomic<shared_ptr>`? | C++20, atomic replace/read of one `shared_ptr` object; usually not lock-free. |

#### Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Atomic vs ordering? | Atomicity protects the variable; memory order defines what it publishes about other memory. |
| What does release do? | Makes every earlier write in the thread visible to any thread whose acquire reads this store's value. |
| What does acquire do? | If it reads a value from a release, everything before that release happens-before everything after this acquire. |
| Does acquire wait? | No. It reads whatever is there; only reading the released value synchronizes. |
| Relaxed publication with plain data? | Data race on the payload: undefined behaviour, not "maybe prints 0". |
| Why is relaxed fine for counters? | RMWs read the latest value in the modification order; nothing else is published. |
| What does seq_cst add? | A single total order of all seq_cst ops, which forbids store-load reordering. |
| Does seq_cst pick which thread runs first? | No, it restricts allowed outcomes, not scheduling. |
| Does release flush the store buffer? | C++ does not say; it defines happens-before. Hardware chooses the mechanism. |
| volatile vs atomic? | volatile = perform every access (MMIO, signals); atomic = atomicity + inter-thread ordering. |
| How does a mutex order memory? | Lock is acquire, unlock is release; unlock synchronizes-with the next lock. |
| x86 vs ARM? | x86 only reorders store→load; ARM reorders everything; C++ orders hide the difference. |
| consume? | Promoted to acquire by every compiler, deprecated in C++26; just use acquire. |
| Fences? | Upgrade nearby relaxed atomics; need an atomic carrying the value; release fence before the store, acquire fence after the load. |

#### Spinlocks, Busy-Waiting and Backoff
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Spinlock vs mutex? | Spinlock burns CPU to avoid sleep/wake cost; a mutex sleeps. Spin only for tiny sections on dedicated cores. |
| Can two threads both acquire? | No: atomic RMWs on one object are totally ordered; only one reads `false`. |
| Why TTAS? | Spinning on an RMW keeps stealing the cache line; spinning on a load keeps a shared copy. |
| What does `pause` do? | Spin-wait hint: saves power, helps the SMT sibling, avoids a pipeline flush on loop exit. |
| Memory orders? | Acquire on lock, release on unlock; relaxed is only OK for the test load. |
| Holder preempted? | Waiters spin away whole time slices; oversubscription makes spinlocks catastrophically slow. |
| Priority inversion? | High-priority spinner on the holder's core never lets the holder run: livelock. |
| Hybrid mutex? | Spin briefly, then sleep on a futex; unlock wakes only if someone sleeps. |
| Does `std::mutex` spin? | Implementation-defined; glibc's default mutex goes straight to futex wait. |
| Better than a spinlock on a hot path? | Often no lock at all: SPSC queue, seqlock, double buffering, per-thread data. |

#### Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Lock-free vs wait-free? | Lock-free: somebody always progresses. Wait-free: everybody progresses in bounded steps. |
| Is a CAS loop wait-free? | No, lock-free; one thread can retry forever. |
| Is a spinlock lock-free? | No, it is blocking: a preempted holder stops everyone. |
| What is ABA? | A value changes A to B to A, so CAS succeeds although the state it depended on changed. |
| How to fix ABA? | Version/tag counter in the CAS word, or never free/reuse a node while any thread may hold it. |
| Do tags fix use-after-free? | No; only type-stable memory or a reclamation scheme does. |
| Does a null check help? | No; dangling pointers are non-null. |
| Hazard pointers in one line? | Announce the pointer, re-validate, and reclaimers skip announced nodes. |
| EBR in one line? | Free a retired node once every thread has left the epoch it was retired in. |
| Is lock-free faster? | Not necessarily; same hot cache line, retries, reclamation cost; benefit is progress and tail latency. |
| Lowest-risk low-latency alternative? | SPSC ring buffers per producer/consumer pair: wait-free, preallocated, no ABA, no reclamation. |

#### Concurrent Queues and Ring Buffers
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Why no mutex in SPSC? | Each index has a single writer; atomics only publish it to the other side. |
| Why release on `tail`? | It publishes the element written before it to the consumer's acquire load. |
| Why release on `head`? | It guarantees the consumer finished reading before the producer reuses the slot. |
| Why power of two? | Wrap with a mask; mandatory if you mask, minor speed-up for constant N. |
| What does `alignas` buy? | No false sharing; no synchronization. |
| Why is MPSC harder? | Reservation and publication are separate events, so `tail` no longer means "ready". |
| Is Vyukov's bounded MPMC lock-free? | No: a producer stalled between reserve and publish blocks consumers at that slot. |
| What does `cv.wait` do with the mutex? | Releases it atomically while waiting, reacquires it before rechecking the predicate. |
| Queue is full, now what? | Policy from data semantics: block, fail, drop, conflate; never silently overwrite incremental data. |
| Make the queue bigger? | Absorbs bursts only; depth is latency; fix sustained mismatch in the consumer. |
| Mutex always a syscall? | No, only when contended after the user-space fast path fails. |

#### async, future/promise, thread_local and call_once
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| promise vs future? | Producer and consumer ends of one shared state carrying a value or exception. |
| Does `get()` wait for the thread to exit? | No, only for the result to be ready. |
| `get()` twice? | UB on `std::future` (libstdc++ throws `no_state`); use `shared_future`. |
| Promise destroyed unset? | Future gets `broken_promise`. |
| Default `std::async` policy? | `async \| deferred`, implementation picks; may never run. |
| Discarded `std::async` future? | Destructor blocks: runs synchronously. |
| `std::async` in a hot path? | No: thread creation, allocation, scheduling jitter. Use a pinned pool/queue. |
| Why a thread pool? | Amortize thread creation, cap concurrency; must handle backpressure. |
| What is `thread_local`? | Thread storage duration: one instance per thread. |
| `thread_local` lifetime? | Per thread: lazily or at first use, destroyed at that thread's exit. |
| `call_once` vs if-flag? | call_once synchronizes, waits, publishes, retries on throw; the if-flag races. |
| `call_once` callable throws? | Flag not set; the next call retries. |
| Magic static or `call_once`? | Static for one lazily built object; call_once for arbitrary or per-object once. |

#### C++20 Synchronization: latch, barrier, semaphore, jthread
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Latch vs barrier? | Latch: one-shot countdown, anyone counts or waits. Barrier: reusable phases for a fixed set of participants, with a completion step. |
| Can a latch be reset? | No; make a new one or use a barrier. |
| Do I need a mutex to read worker results after `latch.wait()`? | No; `count_down` happens-before the return from `wait`. |
| Where does a barrier completion run? | On one participating thread, once per phase, before anyone is released. |
| Semaphore vs mutex? | Semaphore counts permits and has no owner; mutex enforces ownership. |
| Semaphore vs CV? | Semaphore remembers releases; a CV forgets notifications. |
| What does `atomic::wait(old)` do? | Sleeps while the value equals `old`; returns only after seeing a different value. |
| `jthread` vs `thread`? | `jthread` requests stop and joins in its destructor; `thread` calls `terminate` if still joinable. |
| Does `request_stop` interrupt? | No; it sets the stop state and runs callbacks; code must poll or use stop-aware waits. |
| Where does a `stop_callback` run? | In the thread calling `request_stop`, or immediately in the constructor if stop was already requested. |

topics.topic: std::thread: Creation, Lifetime and Argument Passing

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A `std::thread` object is an **owning handle** to a thread of execution, much like `std::unique_ptr` is an owning handle to a heap object.
- Two separate things with two separate lifetimes:
  - the **thread of execution** (OS thread running your callable)
  - the **`std::thread` object** (a C++ object on your stack or in a member)
- The handle must be told what to do with the thread before the handle dies: `join()` (wait for it) or `detach()` (give up ownership).
- If you forget, the destructor calls `std::terminate()`. This is deliberate: C++ refuses to guess between "silently wait" and "silently abandon".
- Arguments are **copied into the new thread's own storage** by default. Reference semantics must be requested explicitly with `std::ref`.
- `std::jthread` (C++20) is the RAII version: its destructor requests stop and joins.

subsections.title: 2. Creating a thread and when it starts running
subsections.content:
- `std::thread t(f, args...);` creates a new thread of execution that calls `std::invoke(copy_of_f, copies_of_args...)`.
- The copies of `f` and `args` are made **in the constructing thread**, before the constructor returns.
- The standard guarantees: completion of the constructor **synchronizes-with** the start of the callable in the new thread.
  - Everything the creating thread wrote before constructing `t` is visible to the new thread. No extra synchronization needed for that.
- The standard does **not** guarantee that the new thread has executed any instruction by the time the constructor returns. Scheduling is up to the OS.
- If the OS cannot create the thread, the constructor throws `std::system_error` (typically `resource_unavailable_try_again`). Then there is no thread to join.
- A default-constructed `std::thread` has no thread: `joinable() == false`.
- Most vexing parse trap: `std::thread t(Task());` declares a **function** named `t`. Use `std::thread t{Task{}};` or `std::thread t((Task()));`.

subsections.title: 3. Lifetime: joinable, join, detach, destructor
subsections.content:
- `joinable()` is true when the object **owns a thread that has not been joined or detached**. It says nothing about whether the thread is still running.

| Operation | Effect on calling thread | `joinable()` after | Thread of execution |
|---|---|---|---|
| construct with callable | returns immediately | `true` | starts (eventually) |
| `join()` | blocks until the thread finishes | `false` | finished and reaped |
| `detach()` | returns immediately | `false` | keeps running, unowned |
| move from `t1` into `t2` | none | `t1` false, `t2` true | unchanged |
| thread function returns | none | **still `true`** | finished, not reaped |
| destructor while joinable | `std::terminate()` | n/a | n/a |
| move-assign onto a joinable thread | `std::terminate()` | n/a | n/a |

- `join()` also gives a **happens-before** edge: completion of the thread synchronizes-with the return of `join()`. Everything the worker wrote is visible after `join()`.
- `join()` on a non-joinable thread throws `std::system_error` (`invalid_argument`). A thread joining itself throws `resource_deadlock_would_occur`.
- `detach()` is a lifetime contract: you promise that everything the detached thread touches outlives it. Use it rarely and deliberately.
- `std::thread` is **move-only**: copying would mean two owners of one OS thread (who joins?).

subsections.title: 4. Argument passing
subsections.content:
- Rule: each argument is **decay-copied** (or moved, for rvalues) into storage owned by the new thread. The callable then receives those stored objects **as rvalues**.
- Consequences:

| Callable parameter | Argument passed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `int x` | `value` | ✅ copy, original untouched |
| `int& x` | `value` | ❌ compile error (rvalue cannot bind to non-const lvalue reference) |
| `const int& x` | `value` | ✅ compiles, but binds to the thread's **internal copy**, not to `value` |
| `int& x` | `std::ref(value)` | ✅ refers to the original; original must outlive the use |
| `int x` | `std::ref(value)` | ✅ `reference_wrapper` converts, `x` is a copy of the value at call time |
| `std::unique_ptr<T> p` | `std::move(ptr)` | ✅ moved into thread storage, then into the parameter |
| `std::string s` | `char buf[]` | ⚠️ only the **pointer** is copied; the `std::string` is built later in the new thread (dangling risk) |

- Arrays and functions decay: `char buf[64]` is stored as `char*`. Conversions to the parameter type happen **in the new thread**, possibly after the buffer is gone.
- Fix for conversions: convert before construction, e.g. `std::thread t(f, std::string(buf));`.
- Member functions: `std::thread t(&Widget::run, &w, 42);` (pointer or `std::ref` to the object, which must outlive the thread). A lambda `[&w]{ w.run(42); }` is usually clearer.
- Lambda captures follow the same idea: `[value]` copies, `[&value]` and `[this]` store references/pointers. `[this]` does **not** copy the object.

subsections.title: 5. Exceptions and threads
subsections.content:
- An exception that escapes the thread's callable calls `std::terminate()`. It is **not** delivered to the thread that created or joins it.
- To propagate: catch in the worker, store `std::current_exception()` into a `std::exception_ptr`, rethrow after `join()` with `std::rethrow_exception`. Or use `std::promise` / `std::packaged_task` / `std::async`, which do this for you.
- Exception safety of the **creating** thread: if code between creating `t` and `t.join()` throws, stack unwinding destroys a joinable `t` and the program terminates. Use a RAII guard or `std::jthread`.
- The return value of the thread function is discarded. Use a future, a reference/pointer output parameter, or shared state to return results.

subsections.title: 6. Thread identity
subsections.content:
- `t.get_id()` returns a `std::thread::id`. For a non-joinable `t` it returns a default-constructed id meaning "not any thread".
- `std::this_thread::get_id()` returns the calling thread's id.
- `std::thread::id` is totally ordered and hashable: valid as a key in `std::map` / `std::unordered_map`.
- It is **not** the OS thread id (Linux TID from `gettid()`). For OS-level work (affinity, priority, naming) use `native_handle()` (a `pthread_t` on Linux).
- Ids can be **reused** after a thread is joined; do not treat them as unique forever.

subsections.title: 7. std::jthread (C++20)
subsections.content:
- Same as `std::thread` plus two things:
  - destructor: if joinable, calls `request_stop()` then `join()` (RAII, no terminate)
  - built-in cooperative cancellation: if the callable's first parameter is `std::stop_token`, `jthread` passes one automatically
- `request_stop()` only **requests**: it sets the shared stop state and runs registered `std::stop_callback`s. It never kills the thread.
- The worker must poll `stop_requested()` (or use a `std::condition_variable_any` wait that takes the token) and return voluntarily.
- If the worker is stuck in a long blocking call that does not observe the token, the `jthread` destructor still blocks in `join()`.

subsections.title: 8. How many threads: hardware_concurrency, cost, oversubscription
subsections.content:
- `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` returns a **hint**: typically the number of online logical CPUs (hardware threads, including SMT/Hyper-Threading). It may return `0` if unknown.
- On Linux it does not reflect CPU affinity masks or container CPU quotas, so in containers it can overstate available CPUs.
- CPU-bound work: start near the number of logical CPUs available to the process, then **benchmark**. SMT siblings share execution units and caches, so 2 logical CPUs are not 2 full cores.
