subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A spinlock is a lock whose waiters **keep running** and re-check the lock instead of going to sleep.
- A blocking mutex says "wake me when it is free"; a spinlock says "I will keep asking, it should be free any moment".
- It trades CPU time for wake-up latency:

| | Spinlock | Blocking mutex (futex-based) |
|---|---|---|
| Waiter state | Running, burning its core | Asleep in the kernel |
| Cost when uncontended | One atomic RMW to lock, one store to unlock | One atomic RMW to lock, one RMW to unlock (no syscall) |
| Cost of a short wait | Tens to hundreds of ns, no syscall | Syscall + context switch + wake-up (microseconds) |
| Cost of a long wait | Wastes a whole core the entire time | Nearly free while asleep |
| Holder preempted | Disaster: waiters spin for a full time slice | Fine: waiters sleep |

- Rule of thumb: spinning only pays when the expected wait is shorter than the cost of sleeping and waking (roughly a few microseconds) **and** the lock holder is guaranteed to be running on another core.

subsections.title: 2. A minimal correct spinlock
3. Why naive spinning hurts: cache-line ping-pong
subsections.content:
- Every `exchange`/`test_and_set` is a **write**, even when it writes `true` over `true`.
- To write, a core needs the cache line in an exclusive state, so with N waiters the line is bounced between cores on every attempt (coherence traffic, MESI-style invalidations).
- Consequences:
  - the interconnect is flooded, slowing unrelated memory traffic on the same line or socket;
  - the **unlocking** store has to fight the same traffic, so the holder releases later;
  - throughput collapses as waiters increase.
- C++ vs hardware: the C++ guarantee is "the RMW is atomic"; cache coherence is how the hardware happens to provide it. Explain correctness in C++ terms, performance in hardware terms.

subsections.title: 4. Test-and-test-and-set (TTAS)
5. `pause`, `yield` and backoff
subsections.content:
- `cpu_relax()` inside the spin loop:
  - x86: `pause` (`_mm_pause()`): tells the core this is a spin-wait. It saves power, frees resources for the hyper-threaded sibling, and avoids a pipeline flush (memory-order mis-speculation) when the loop exits.
  - Latency varies: about 10 cycles on older Intel cores, about 140 cycles on Skylake and several later cores. Tune spin counts in time, not iterations.
  - ARM: `yield` (some runtimes use `isb` instead).
- `std::this_thread::yield()`: a syscall that offers the CPU to another runnable thread. Weak guarantee (the scheduler may run you again immediately), but useful after spinning for a while.
- Exponential backoff: after each failed attempt wait 2x longer (capped), then yield. It spreads out the RMW bursts and reduces contention, at the cost of fairness and some latency.
- Fair alternatives: ticket locks (FIFO via two counters) and queue locks (MCS/CLH, each waiter spins on its own cache line). The Linux kernel's `qspinlock` is MCS-based.

subsections.title: 6. When spinning beats sleeping
7. Preemption and priority inversion
subsections.content:
- User-space spinlocks cannot stop the OS from preempting the holder.
  - Holder is preempted inside the critical section: every waiter spins uselessly until the holder is scheduled again, typically a full time slice (milliseconds).
  - Kernel spinlocks avoid this by disabling preemption (and optionally interrupts) while held; user space cannot.
- Priority inversion with real-time priorities:
  - low-priority thread L holds the spinlock; high-priority `SCHED_FIFO` thread H on the **same core** starts spinning;
  - H never blocks, so the scheduler never runs L, so L never releases: a livelock.
  - If L is also a lower-priority `SCHED_FIFO` thread, nothing ever lets it run. If L is a normal (`SCHED_OTHER`) thread, Linux RT throttling (by default RT tasks may use 95% of each second) leaves it a small slice, so it crawls forward.
  - A blocking mutex lets H sleep, so L runs. `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` mutexes go further and boost L. Spinlocks are invisible to the kernel, so no inheritance is possible.
- Single-core machines: spinning is pure waste, because the holder cannot run while you spin.

subsections.title: 8. Hybrid (spin-then-sleep) mutexes
subsections.content:
- Idea: spin briefly in user space (the holder will probably release soon); if not, sleep in the kernel.
- Linux building block: the **futex** (fast userspace mutex). The lock word lives in user memory; the kernel is called only to sleep (`FUTEX_WAIT`, which sleeps only if the word still has the expected value) or to wake (`FUTEX_WAKE`).
- Classic 3-state design: `0` = free, `1` = locked, `2` = locked with possible sleepers. Unlock only issues the wake syscall if the state was `2`.
- Typical implementation facts (glibc, Linux):
  - `std::mutex` maps to a default `pthread_mutex_t`: uncontended lock/unlock is a single atomic op in user space, contended lock goes to `futex_wait` **without** spinning.
  - `PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP` spins a bounded number of times before sleeping (spin count tunable via the `glibc.pthread.mutex_spin_count` tunable).
  - Windows `CRITICAL_SECTION` has a configurable spin count; `SRWLOCK` spins briefly.
- C++20 gives a portable building block: `std::atomic<T>::wait/notify_one` (and `atomic_flag::wait`) are futex-like, so a hybrid lock can be written without platform APIs.

subsections.title: 9. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Spinlocks are faster than mutexes." ✅ Only for very short, rarely contended sections on dedicated cores; oversubscribed they can be 10x to 20x slower.
- ❌ "Low latency means use spinlocks." ✅ Low latency means avoid sharing; prefer lock-free hand-off structures, then consider spinning.
- ❌ "Waiters in `while (exchange(true))` are only reading." ✅ Each `exchange` is a write that demands cache-line ownership; spin on a load (TTAS).
- ❌ "`relaxed` is enough because the flag is atomic." ✅ Lock needs acquire, unlock needs release, or the protected data races.
- ❌ "A `volatile bool` works as a spinlock flag." ✅ `volatile` gives neither atomicity nor ordering; it is a data race.
- ❌ "Atomics work because MESI locks the cache line." ✅ The C++ memory model defines the guarantee; coherence protocols are one way hardware implements it.
- ❌ "`std::mutex` spins before sleeping." ✅ Implementation-defined; glibc's default mutex does not spin at all.
- ❌ "If the holder gets preempted, waiters just wait a bit longer." ✅ They burn whole time slices, and with real-time priorities on one core they can livelock forever.
- ❌ "A spinlock is safe to use like a recursive mutex." ✅ Re-locking from the same thread spins forever (self-deadlock).

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- A spinlock is a lock whose waiters **keep running** and re-check the lock instead of going to sleep.
- A blocking mutex says "wake me when it is free"; a spinlock says "I will keep asking, it should be free any moment".
- It trades CPU time for wake-up latency:

| | Spinlock | Blocking mutex (futex-based) |
|---|---|---|
| Waiter state | Running, burning its core | Asleep in the kernel |
| Cost when uncontended | One atomic RMW to lock, one store to unlock | One atomic RMW to lock, one RMW to unlock (no syscall) |
| Cost of a short wait | Tens to hundreds of ns, no syscall | Syscall + context switch + wake-up (microseconds) |
| Cost of a long wait | Wastes a whole core the entire time | Nearly free while asleep |
| Holder preempted | Disaster: waiters spin for a full time slice | Fine: waiters sleep |

- Rule of thumb: spinning only pays when the expected wait is shorter than the cost of sleeping and waking (roughly a few microseconds) **and** the lock holder is guaranteed to be running on another core.

#### 2. A minimal correct spinlock
- Acquire = an atomic read-modify-write that sets "locked" and tells you the previous value.
  - `std::atomic_flag::test_and_set()` or `std::atomic<bool>::exchange(true)`.
  - If the old value was `false`, you own the lock; otherwise somebody else does, so retry.
- Release = a plain atomic store of `false`.
- Memory ordering:
  - `lock()`: `memory_order_acquire` on the successful RMW, so critical-section reads/writes cannot move above it and you see the previous holder's writes.
  - `unlock()`: `memory_order_release`, so your critical-section writes are visible to the next acquirer.
  - Anything weaker (`relaxed`) gives mutual exclusion on the flag but **not** protection of the data: the data accesses become a data race.
- Two threads can never both acquire it: RMW operations on one atomic object are totally ordered (its modification order), and each RMW reads the value written by the previous one in that order. Only one of them can read `false`.
- Name the members `lock()`, `unlock()` (and `try_lock()`) so `std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_lock` and `std::scoped_lock` work with it. Never call them by hand without RAII: an exception would leave it locked forever.

```cpp
class SpinLock {
    std::atomic_flag flag_;                 // C++20: default-initialized to clear
public:
    void lock()     { while (flag_.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire)) {} }
    bool try_lock() { return !flag_.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire); }
    void unlock()   { flag_.clear(std::memory_order_release); }
};
```

#### 3. Why naive spinning hurts: cache-line ping-pong
- Every `exchange`/`test_and_set` is a **write**, even when it writes `true` over `true`.
- To write, a core needs the cache line in an exclusive state, so with N waiters the line is bounced between cores on every attempt (coherence traffic, MESI-style invalidations).
- Consequences:
  - the interconnect is flooded, slowing unrelated memory traffic on the same line or socket;
  - the **unlocking** store has to fight the same traffic, so the holder releases later;
  - throughput collapses as waiters increase.
- C++ vs hardware: the C++ guarantee is "the RMW is atomic"; cache coherence is how the hardware happens to provide it. Explain correctness in C++ terms, performance in hardware terms.

#### 4. Test-and-test-and-set (TTAS)
- Spin on a plain **load** while the lock is held; attempt the RMW only when it looks free.

```cpp
void lock() {
    while (true) {
        if (!locked_.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) return;  // try
        while (locked_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) cpu_relax();     // test
    }
}
```

- Loads let every waiter keep a **shared** copy of the line in its own cache; no traffic while the holder works.
- On unlock the line is invalidated once, everyone reloads, and a burst of RMWs follows (one wins). This burst is why TTAS still degrades with many waiters.
- The relaxed load is fine: it is only a hint. Correctness comes from the acquire RMW.
- C++20 `std::atomic_flag::test()` allows TTAS with `atomic_flag` too.

#### 5. `pause`, `yield` and backoff
- `cpu_relax()` inside the spin loop:
  - x86: `pause` (`_mm_pause()`): tells the core this is a spin-wait. It saves power, frees resources for the hyper-threaded sibling, and avoids a pipeline flush (memory-order mis-speculation) when the loop exits.
  - Latency varies: about 10 cycles on older Intel cores, about 140 cycles on Skylake and several later cores. Tune spin counts in time, not iterations.
  - ARM: `yield` (some runtimes use `isb` instead).
- `std::this_thread::yield()`: a syscall that offers the CPU to another runnable thread. Weak guarantee (the scheduler may run you again immediately), but useful after spinning for a while.
- Exponential backoff: after each failed attempt wait 2x longer (capped), then yield. It spreads out the RMW bursts and reduces contention, at the cost of fairness and some latency.
- Fair alternatives: ticket locks (FIFO via two counters) and queue locks (MCS/CLH, each waiter spins on its own cache line). The Linux kernel's `qspinlock` is MCS-based.

#### 6. When spinning beats sleeping
- Spinning can win when **all** hold:
  - the critical section is tiny (tens to hundreds of ns, no syscalls, no allocation, no I/O);
  - threads are **pinned** to dedicated cores, with no more runnable threads than cores (no oversubscription);
  - the cost of a sleep/wake (syscall + context switch, a few microseconds, plus cache pollution) is unacceptable, as on a low-latency hot path.
- Spinning loses when:
  - hold times are long or unpredictable (a 10 ms section means waiters burn 10 ms of CPU each);
  - threads outnumber cores: the holder gets preempted and waiters spin away their entire time slices;
  - the machine is shared (containers, laptops, power-limited cores).
- Measured example (20 logical CPUs, 8 threads, tiny section): TTAS ≈ 0.6 to 0.8 s, TAS ≈ 0.9 to 1.3 s, `std::mutex` ≈ 0.9 s. With **80** threads: TAS ≈ 16 to 19 s, TTAS ≈ 3.3 to 4 s, `std::mutex` ≈ 0.8 to 0.9 s. Oversubscription turns spinlocks from "slightly faster" into "20x slower".
- Before reaching for a spinlock on a hot path, ask whether a lock is needed at all: SPSC queues, seqlocks, double buffering or per-thread data often remove it.

#### 7. Preemption and priority inversion
- User-space spinlocks cannot stop the OS from preempting the holder.
  - Holder is preempted inside the critical section: every waiter spins uselessly until the holder is scheduled again, typically a full time slice (milliseconds).
  - Kernel spinlocks avoid this by disabling preemption (and optionally interrupts) while held; user space cannot.
- Priority inversion with real-time priorities:
  - low-priority thread L holds the spinlock; high-priority `SCHED_FIFO` thread H on the **same core** starts spinning;
  - H never blocks, so the scheduler never runs L, so L never releases: a livelock.
  - If L is also a lower-priority `SCHED_FIFO` thread, nothing ever lets it run. If L is a normal (`SCHED_OTHER`) thread, Linux RT throttling (by default RT tasks may use 95% of each second) leaves it a small slice, so it crawls forward.
  - A blocking mutex lets H sleep, so L runs. `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` mutexes go further and boost L. Spinlocks are invisible to the kernel, so no inheritance is possible.
- Single-core machines: spinning is pure waste, because the holder cannot run while you spin.

#### 8. Hybrid (spin-then-sleep) mutexes
- Idea: spin briefly in user space (the holder will probably release soon); if not, sleep in the kernel.
- Linux building block: the **futex** (fast userspace mutex). The lock word lives in user memory; the kernel is called only to sleep (`FUTEX_WAIT`, which sleeps only if the word still has the expected value) or to wake (`FUTEX_WAKE`).
- Classic 3-state design: `0` = free, `1` = locked, `2` = locked with possible sleepers. Unlock only issues the wake syscall if the state was `2`.
- Typical implementation facts (glibc, Linux):
  - `std::mutex` maps to a default `pthread_mutex_t`: uncontended lock/unlock is a single atomic op in user space, contended lock goes to `futex_wait` **without** spinning.
  - `PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP` spins a bounded number of times before sleeping (spin count tunable via the `glibc.pthread.mutex_spin_count` tunable).
  - Windows `CRITICAL_SECTION` has a configurable spin count; `SRWLOCK` spins briefly.
- C++20 gives a portable building block: `std::atomic<T>::wait/notify_one` (and `atomic_flag::wait`) are futex-like, so a hybrid lock can be written without platform APIs.

#### 9. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "Spinlocks are faster than mutexes." ✅ Only for very short, rarely contended sections on dedicated cores; oversubscribed they can be 10x to 20x slower.
- ❌ "Low latency means use spinlocks." ✅ Low latency means avoid sharing; prefer lock-free hand-off structures, then consider spinning.
- ❌ "Waiters in `while (exchange(true))` are only reading." ✅ Each `exchange` is a write that demands cache-line ownership; spin on a load (TTAS).
- ❌ "`relaxed` is enough because the flag is atomic." ✅ Lock needs acquire, unlock needs release, or the protected data races.
- ❌ "A `volatile bool` works as a spinlock flag." ✅ `volatile` gives neither atomicity nor ordering; it is a data race.
- ❌ "Atomics work because MESI locks the cache line." ✅ The C++ memory model defines the guarantee; coherence protocols are one way hardware implements it.
- ❌ "`std::mutex` spins before sleeping." ✅ Implementation-defined; glibc's default mutex does not spin at all.
- ❌ "If the holder gets preempted, waiters just wait a bit longer." ✅ They burn whole time slices, and with real-time priorities on one core they can livelock forever.
- ❌ "A spinlock is safe to use like a recursive mutex." ✅ Re-locking from the same thread spins forever (self-deadlock).

edge_cases.title: Spinning on a plain or `volatile bool`
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "Reading a bool is atomic on x86, so a `bool` flag is fine".
- What happens: concurrent non-atomic read and write is a data race (undefined behaviour). In practice, at `-O2` the compiler may load the flag once and turn `while (flag) {}` into an infinite loop, or (forward-progress rule) delete the empty loop entirely so the waiter does not wait at all; GCC 11 does the latter. Also, check-then-set on a plain bool lets two threads in.
- `volatile` forces reloads but gives no atomic RMW and no ordering: still a race, still broken.
- Fix: `std::atomic_flag` or `std::atomic<bool>` with acquire/release.

edge_cases.title: Relaxed ordering on lock or unlock
edge_cases.explanation:
- `exchange(true, relaxed)` / `store(false, relaxed)` still lets only one thread "own" the flag.
- But critical-section loads/stores may be reordered across the lock operations, and no happens-before exists between holders: the protected data is raced.
- Often appears to work on x86 (strong hardware ordering) and breaks on ARM/POWER or after compiler reordering.

edge_cases.title: `compare_exchange` without resetting `expected`
Holder preempted while waiters spin (oversubscription)
edge_cases.explanation:
- With more runnable threads than cores, the holder can be descheduled mid-section.
- Waiters then spin for whole time slices, and they are the very threads stopping the holder from being rescheduled.
- Measured on a 20-CPU machine with 80 threads: a TAS spinlock took 16 to 19 s for work a `std::mutex` did in under 1 s.

edge_cases.title: Priority inversion with real-time threads
edge_cases.explanation:
- Low-priority holder, high-priority spinner, same core, `SCHED_FIFO`: the spinner never yields, the holder never runs.
- Result: livelock (permanent if both are `SCHED_FIFO`).
- A blocking mutex (ideally with priority inheritance) does not have this failure mode.

edge_cases.title: Self-deadlock and missing RAII
edge_cases.explanation:
- Calling `lock()` twice on the same thread spins forever; spinlocks are never recursive.
- `lock(); work(); unlock();` with a throwing `work()` leaves the lock held, and every later `lock()` spins forever.
- Fix: `std::lock_guard<SpinLock>`; keep callbacks and anything that may re-enter the lock out of the critical section.

edge_cases.title: The lock shares a cache line with hot data
edge_cases.explanation:
- Waiters hammering the lock word invalidate the line that also holds the data the holder is writing (or unrelated hot fields: false sharing).
- Fix: `alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)` (or `alignas(64)`) for the lock word; ticket locks keep `next` and `serving` on separate lines.

edge_cases.title: Spinning on a single core
edge_cases.explanation:
- If only one core is available (pinned, cgroup-limited, or uniprocessor VM), the holder cannot run while you spin.
- Each acquisition attempt by a waiter costs up to a full time slice. Any spin loop must eventually `yield` or sleep.

code_examples.title: Minimal `atomic_flag` spinlock with RAII
code_examples.explanation:
- `test_and_set` with acquire, `clear` with release, used through `std::lock_guard`.

- Output: `counter=400000` every run.
- `std::atomic_flag` is the only atomic type the standard guarantees to be lock-free.

code_examples.title: TTAS spinlock with `pause`, usable with `std::scoped_lock`
code_examples.explanation:
- Spins on a relaxed load, uses `pause`, and provides `try_lock` so `std::scoped_lock` can lock two of them without deadlock.

- Output: `a=1000 b=1000 total=2000` (each direction moved 100000 units).
- Opposite lock orders in `t1` and `t2` would deadlock with naive nested locking; `std::scoped_lock` uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm that relies on `try_lock`.

code_examples.title: Exponential backoff, then yield
code_examples.explanation:
- Spreads out retries under contention; after a cap it yields the CPU.

- Output: `counter=800000`.
- Backoff improves throughput under contention but is unfair: a thread that just released (and has no backoff) tends to re-acquire first.

code_examples.title: Hybrid spin-then-sleep mutex with C++20 `atomic::wait`
code_examples.explanation:
- Bounded spinning, then a futex-style sleep. State `2` means "someone may be sleeping, unlock must wake".

- Output: `counter=1600000`.
- This is the classic three-state futex mutex. `atomic::wait(2)` only blocks if the value is still `2`, so a concurrent unlock cannot be missed.

code_examples.title: Ticket lock (FIFO fairness)
code_examples.explanation:
- Each waiter takes a ticket; the lock serves tickets in order, so no thread can starve.

- Output: `counter=400000`.
- Downside: strict FIFO hurts under oversubscription. If the next ticket holder is descheduled, everybody waits for it ("convoy").

- With threads ≤ cores, TTAS edges out the mutex. Oversubscribed, the spinlocks lose by 4x to 20x because waiters burn the CPU that preempted holders need.

interview_qa.question: What is a spinlock, and how does it differ from a `std::mutex`?
interview_qa.answer: A spinlock is a lock whose waiters keep running and re-check the lock in a loop instead of sleeping. A mutex puts contended waiters to sleep in the kernel. Spinning avoids the sleep/wake cost but burns a CPU for the whole wait.

interview_qa.question: What does the x86 `pause` instruction do in a spin loop, and when should a spinner yield or back off instead?
interview_qa.answer: `pause` is a spin-wait hint: it slows the loop, saves power, frees execution resources for the hyper-threaded sibling and avoids a costly pipeline flush when the loop exits. After a bounded spin, back off exponentially and then yield or sleep.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Without `pause`, a tight load loop fills the pipeline with speculative loads; when the lock word changes the CPU detects a memory-order violation and flushes.
- Latency differs by CPU: about 10 cycles on older Intel cores, about 140 cycles on Skylake and several later cores. Calibrate spin budgets in time, not iteration counts.
- Exponential backoff: wait 1, 2, 4, ... pauses between attempts (capped), which spreads retries and reduces contention.
- `std::this_thread::yield()`: lets another runnable thread (possibly the preempted holder) run; weak guarantees.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`pause` puts the thread to sleep." It is a few to ~140 cycles of delay; the thread stays on the CPU.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: on ARM use `yield` (or `isb`); C++ has no portable `cpu_relax`, so wrap the intrinsic.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `pause` for every spin iteration; backoff and yield once the spin is clearly not short.

interview_qa.question: What happens if the thread holding a spinlock is preempted?
interview_qa.answer: All waiters keep spinning until the holder is scheduled again, often a full time slice of milliseconds, burning CPU that the holder itself may need. With more runnable threads than cores this cascades, and spinlocks become far slower than a blocking mutex.
interview_qa.explanation:
- User-space code cannot disable preemption, so any spinlock holder can be descheduled mid-section.
- Waiters occupy cores (and run queues), delaying the holder's return.
- Measured: 80 threads on 20 CPUs, tiny section: TAS spinlock 16 to 19 s, `std::mutex` under 1 s.
- Ticket locks make it worse: if the **next** ticket holder is preempted, everyone waits for it (convoy).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Waiters just wait a bit longer." They waste whole time slices and amplify the delay.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: Linux kernel spinlocks disable preemption (and optionally interrupts) while held, which is why spinlocks are standard inside the kernel but risky in user space; in user space, pin threads to dedicated cores or use a hybrid lock.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A spinlock assumes the holder is running; preemption breaks that assumption badly.

interview_qa.question: How can a spinlock cause priority inversion or livelock with real-time threads?
interview_qa.answer: If a low-priority thread holds the spinlock and a higher-priority `SCHED_FIFO` thread on the same core spins for it, the spinner never blocks, so the scheduler never runs the holder, which never releases. A blocking mutex (ideally with priority inheritance) lets the holder run.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Real-time `SCHED_FIFO` threads run until they block or yield; a higher-priority one always preempts a lower one on the same CPU.
- Both `SCHED_FIFO`: permanent livelock.
- Holder is a normal `SCHED_OTHER` thread: Linux RT throttling (default 95% of each second for RT tasks) leaves it a little CPU, so the system crawls instead of freezing.
- Mutex with `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`: the kernel temporarily boosts the holder to the waiter's priority. Impossible with a spinlock, because the kernel does not know the lock exists.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Priority inversion only affects mutexes." Spinlocks make it worse: the high-priority thread does not even sleep.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: real-time systems avoid user-space spinlocks across priority levels on shared cores, or bound the spin and fall back to blocking.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Spinning plus strict priorities on one core can stop the holder from ever running.

interview_qa.question: How does a hybrid "spin-then-sleep" mutex work, and does `std::mutex` spin?
interview_qa.answer: It spins briefly in user space, betting the holder releases soon, then sleeps on a futex. A 3-state word (free, locked, locked with sleepers) lets unlock skip the wake syscall when nobody sleeps. On glibc, `std::mutex` does not spin; the adaptive pthread mutex type does.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Hybrid lock = short spin for the common case, futex sleep for the long tail.

interview_qa.question: `std::atomic_flag` or `std::atomic<bool>` for a spinlock? What changed in C++20?
interview_qa.answer: `atomic_flag` is the only type guaranteed lock-free, but before C++20 it had only `test_and_set` and `clear`, so TTAS needed `atomic<bool>`. C++20 adds `test()`, `wait()` and `notify_one/all()` and default-initializes it to clear, making either type fine.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Pre-C++20: `std::atomic_flag f = ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT;` was required; no plain read existed.
- C++20: `std::atomic_flag f;` is clear; `f.test()` enables TTAS; `f.wait(true)` enables a sleeping fallback.
- `std::atomic<bool>` is lock-free on every mainstream platform (`is_always_lock_free`), but the standard only guarantees it for `atomic_flag`.
- Either way, align the lock to its own cache line if it sits next to hot data.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`volatile bool` is enough." `volatile` provides neither atomic RMW nor inter-thread ordering; it is a data race.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: lock-free matters for spinlocks because a lock-based "atomic" would hide a real mutex inside your spinlock.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Use `atomic_flag` (C++20 API) or `atomic<bool>`; never a plain or `volatile` bool.

interview_qa.question: What is a ticket lock and what problem does it solve?
interview_qa.answer: A ticket lock has two counters: a waiter takes `my = next.fetch_add(1)` and spins until `serving == my`; unlock increments `serving`. It grants the lock in FIFO order, preventing the starvation that TAS/TTAS allow, at the cost of convoys if a waiting thread is preempted.
interview_qa.explanation:
- TAS/TTAS are unfair: the releasing thread, with the line hot in its cache, often re-acquires immediately.
- Ticket lock waiters only **load** `serving` while waiting; one RMW per acquisition (`fetch_add` on `next`).
- Only the holder writes `serving`, so `store(load + 1, release)` is enough in `unlock`.
- Downsides:
  - all waiters still spin on one cache line (invalidated on every release);
  - strict order: if the next ticket's thread is descheduled, nobody else can proceed.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Fair means faster." Fairness usually costs throughput.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: MCS/CLH queue locks keep FIFO order and let each waiter spin on its own cache line; the Linux `qspinlock` is built on MCS.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Ticket locks trade throughput for FIFO fairness; queue locks fix the shared-line spinning.

interview_qa.question: A market-data thread updates a small quote (bid, ask, sizes) that a strategy thread reads. Would you protect it with a spinlock?
interview_qa.answer: A spinlock is defensible: the section is a few stores, threads are usually pinned, and sleeping would cost more than the wait. But the better answer often removes the lock: a seqlock, double buffering, or an SPSC queue lets the reader never block the writer.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Why a spinlock can be OK here: tiny section, two threads, dedicated cores, no syscalls inside.
- Why it is not ideal:
  - the reader can delay the writer, and the writer is the latency-critical side;
  - both threads hammer the same cache line.
- Lock-free alternatives:
  - **seqlock:** writer increments a sequence counter (odd = writing), writes, increments again; reader retries if the sequence was odd or changed. The writer never waits.
  - **double buffer / snapshot index:** writer fills the inactive copy and publishes its index with a release store.
  - **SPSC ring buffer:** if the reader needs every update, not just the latest.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Latency matters, so use a spinlock." First ask whether shared mutable state is needed at all.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: whichever you choose, put the lock/sequence word and the data on cache lines that the reader does not write.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: For hot single-writer data, prefer designs where the writer never waits; a spinlock is the fallback, not the goal.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.answer: Data race on `counter`: undefined behaviour. It typically still prints counter=400000 on x86, which hides the bug.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The flag itself is fine: only one thread at a time sees `exchange` return `false`.
- But with `relaxed`, the unlock does not synchronize-with the next lock, so there is no happens-before between one holder's `++counter` and the next holder's read. Conflicting non-atomic accesses without happens-before = data race.
- The compiler may also move `++counter` across relaxed atomic operations.
- x86 hardware is strongly ordered and GCC rarely moves code across atomics, so tests pass; on ARM/POWER, or with a different compiler, updates can be lost.
- ThreadSanitizer reports a data race on `counter` for this program; the fixed version is clean.
- **Key Concept:** A lock needs acquire on lock and release on unlock; atomicity of the flag alone does not protect the data.
practice_tasks.key_concept: A lock needs acquire on lock and release on unlock; atomicity of the flag alone does not protect the data.
additional_code: Data race on `counter`: undefined behaviour. It typically still prints counter=400000 on x86, which hides the bug.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.answer: Mutual exclusion is broken (data race, undefined behaviour). It typically prints a value below 4000000, different on every run.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- On failure, `compare_exchange_weak` stores the **current** value into `expected`. Once the lock is seen held, `expected` becomes `true`.
- The next iteration is `CAS(expected = true → true)`, which **succeeds** while another thread holds the lock. Two threads are now in the critical section.
- Lost `++counter` updates show up as a final count below 4000000 (for example `counter=3999xxx` or much lower).
- ThreadSanitizer reports the race on `counter`.
- **Key Concept:** In a CAS loop, reset `expected` on every failure (or use `exchange`, which has no `expected`).
practice_tasks.key_concept: In a CAS loop, reset `expected` on every failure (or use `exchange`, which has no `expected`).
additional_code: Mutual exclusion is broken (data race, undefined behaviour). It typically prints a value below 4000000, different on every run.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer: Not correct: two threads can enter together (data race, undefined behaviour). It typically prints a value below 4000000.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- "Load, then store" is a check-then-act sequence, not an atomic RMW. Two threads can both load `false` and both store `true`.
- Every individual operation is atomic, yet the **pair** is not; fences cannot fix that.
- In real TTAS the load is only a hint; acquisition must still be an RMW (`exchange` or CAS) that can fail.
- **Key Concept:** Test with a load, set with an RMW.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Test with a load, set with an RMW.
additional_code: Not correct: two threads can enter together (data race, undefined behaviour). It typically prints a value below 4000000.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer: Data race: undefined behaviour. With g++ 11 -O2 it prints "waiter sees data=0" immediately; other compilers or flags may instead spin forever.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `locked` and `data` are shared without atomics or locks: a data race, so the optimizer may assume no other thread modifies them.
- The loop body has no side effects, and C++ lets the compiler assume such a loop terminates (forward-progress rule). GCC 11 at `-O2` deletes the loop completely: `waiter` prints at once, long before `main` writes `42`.
- Another legal outcome: load `locked` once and turn the loop into `for (;;) {}`, a hang. Both are "correct" compilations of a racy program.
- `volatile bool` would force a reload each iteration but still gives no ordering for `data` and no atomic RMW for building a real lock: still a data race.
- **Key Concept:** Any flag shared between threads must be `std::atomic` (or protected by a lock); with release/acquire it also publishes the data written before it.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Any flag shared between threads must be `std::atomic` (or protected by a lock); with release/acquire it also publishes the data written before it.
additional_code: Data race: undefined behaviour. With g++ 11 -O2 it prints "waiter sees data=0" immediately; other compilers or flags may instead spin forever.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.answer:
caught: insufficient funds
try_lock after exception: false
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `withdraw` throws between `lock()` and `unlock()`, so `unlock()` never runs.
- The spinlock stays held forever. `try_lock` returns `false`; a real `lock()` call would spin forever and burn a core (unlike a mutex deadlock, which at least sleeps).
- Spinlocks have no owner tracking and no timeout, so this failure is silent.
- **Key Concept:** Always use RAII (`std::lock_guard<SpinLock>`); give your spinlock `lock`/`unlock`/`try_lock` so it works with standard lock wrappers.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Always use RAII (`std::lock_guard<SpinLock>`); give your spinlock `lock`/`unlock`/`try_lock` so it works with standard lock wrappers.

caught: insufficient funds
try_lock after exception: false

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.answer: Yes. It self-deadlocks with a single thread: it spins forever at 100% CPU and prints nothing.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `handle_request` holds the spinlock; `log_hit` tries to take it again on the same thread.
- A spinlock has no owner, so it cannot detect re-entry; the thread waits for itself forever.
- A `std::mutex` would also deadlock here (undefined behaviour), but typically sleeping; the spinlock burns a core while hung.
- Fix by restructuring: an unlocked internal helper called with the lock already held, or move the call outside the critical section. Recursive locks hide design problems; avoid them.
- **Key Concept:** Spinlocks are never recursive; never call code that may take the same lock while holding it.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Spinlocks are never recursive; never call code that may take the same lock while holding it.
additional_code: Yes. It self-deadlocks with a single thread: it spins forever at 100% CPU and prints nothing.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: std::scoped_lock with two locks calls std::lock, which needs try_lock(); SpinLock has no member named 'try_lock'.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::lock_guard` and single-argument `std::scoped_lock` only need **BasicLockable**: `lock()` and `unlock()`.
- Multi-lock `std::scoped_lock` (and `std::lock`) uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm: lock one, `try_lock` the others, back off and retry on failure. That needs **Lockable**: `try_lock()` as well.
- Adding `bool try_lock() { return !flag_.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire); }` fixes it.
- **Key Concept:** Give custom locks the full `lock`/`try_lock`/`unlock` interface so standard RAII wrappers and `std::lock` work.

quick_reference.content:
#### Spinlock variants
| Variant | Spin on | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAS (`exchange` / `test_and_set` loop) | RMW | Simplest | Cache-line ping-pong, collapses under contention |
| TTAS | Relaxed load, RMW when free | Quiet while held | Thundering burst on release; unfair |
| TTAS + backoff | Load + growing pauses + yield | Better throughput under contention | More latency, unfair |
| Ticket lock | Load of `serving` | FIFO fair | All waiters on one line; convoys if a waiter is preempted |
| MCS / CLH queue lock | Own cache line | Scales, fair | More complex, per-waiter node |
| Hybrid (spin then futex) | Bounded spin, then sleep | Good default for user space | Two code paths, tuning |

#### Memory orders for a lock
| Operation | Order | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Successful acquire RMW | `acquire` | See previous holder's writes; keep section after it |
| Spin "test" load | `relaxed` | Only a hint; the RMW re-checks |
| Release store | `release` | Publish section writes to next acquirer |
| CAS failure order | `relaxed` | Failed attempt synchronizes nothing |

#### When to spin
| Condition | Spin? |
|---|---|
| Section < ~1 µs, threads pinned, threads ≤ cores | Possibly |
| Unknown or long hold time, syscalls or I/O inside | No |
| More runnable threads than cores / shared machine | No |
| Real-time priorities sharing a core | Never |
| Single core | Never (or yield immediately) |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Spinlock vs mutex? | Spinlock burns CPU to avoid sleep/wake cost; a mutex sleeps. Spin only for tiny sections on dedicated cores. |
| Can two threads both acquire? | No: atomic RMWs on one object are totally ordered; only one reads `false`. |
| Why TTAS? | Spinning on an RMW keeps stealing the cache line; spinning on a load keeps a shared copy. |
| What does `pause` do? | Spin-wait hint: saves power, helps the SMT sibling, avoids a pipeline flush on loop exit. |
| Memory orders? | Acquire on lock, release on unlock; relaxed is only OK for the test load. |
| Holder preempted? | Waiters spin away whole time slices; oversubscription makes spinlocks catastrophically slow. |
| Priority inversion? | High-priority spinner on the holder's core never lets the holder run: livelock. |
| Hybrid mutex? | Spin briefly, then sleep on a futex; unlock wakes only if someone sleeps. |
| Does `std::mutex` spin? | Implementation-defined; glibc's default mutex goes straight to futex wait. |
| Better than a spinlock on a hot path? | Often no lock at all: SPSC queue, seqlock, double buffering, per-thread data. |

topics.topic: Lock-Free Programming and the ABA Problem

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- "Lock-free" is a **progress guarantee**, not "code without `std::mutex`" and not "fast".
- The test that defines each class: **suspend one thread at the worst possible instruction, forever. Can the others still finish their operations?**
  - Blocking (mutex, spinlock): no, if the suspended thread holds the lock.
  - Lock-free: yes, at least one other thread keeps completing operations.
  - Wait-free: yes, and every running thread finishes within a bounded number of its own steps.
- A lock-free data structure is three problems stacked on top of each other:

| Layer | Question | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| CAS | Is the shared word still what I based my update on? | `compare_exchange` (topic 05) |
| ABA | Did it change away and come back while I was not looking? | tags/version counters, or never reuse memory while it is referenced |
| Memory reclamation | Can another thread still be dereferencing the node I just removed? | hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, RCU, reference counting |

- Writing the CAS loop is the easy 10 percent. ABA and reclamation are where real lock-free code breaks.

subsections.title: 2. Progress guarantees
subsections.content:
| Class | Guarantee | Can one thread starve? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Blocking** | none if a lock holder is delayed | yes | `std::mutex`, spinlock |
| **Obstruction-free** | a thread completes if it eventually runs **in isolation** (others paused) | yes, and livelock among contenders is possible | some STM designs |
| **Lock-free** | **system-wide**: some thread completes an operation in a finite number of steps | yes | CAS retry loop, Treiber stack |
| **Wait-free** | **per-thread**: every operation completes in a bounded number of its own steps | no | SPSC ring buffer `try_push`/`try_pop`, `fetch_add` on x86 (`lock xadd`) |

- Strength: wait-free > lock-free > obstruction-free > blocking. Each implies the ones below it.
- Blocking algorithms are further split into deadlock-free (some thread acquires) and starvation-free (every thread eventually acquires, e.g. a fair ticket lock).
- Lock-freedom is a property of the **whole algorithm**, including the atomics it uses (`is_always_lock_free`) and anything it calls (an allocator that takes a lock breaks it).
- Wait-free does **not** mean low latency; wait-free algorithms are often slower on average (helping, extra metadata). The guarantee is a bound, not a speed.
- Theory footnote: CAS has infinite consensus number (Herlihy), so it can implement any wait-free object; plain loads/stores cannot even solve 2-thread consensus; `fetch_add`, `exchange`, `test_and_set` have consensus number 2.

subsections.title: 3. The Treiber stack (the canonical lock-free structure)
subsections.content:
- Shared state: `std::atomic<Node*> head`.
- **Push**:
```text
n->next = head.load()
loop: CAS(head, expected = n->next, desired = n)   // on failure n->next is refreshed
```
- **Pop**:
```text
old = head.load()
loop: if old == null: empty
      next = old->next           <-- dereferences old: lifetime problem
      CAS(head, expected = old, desired = next)
return old
```
- Linearization point: the successful CAS on `head`.
- Push is easy and safe: it only dereferences its own node.
- Pop is hard: it reads `old->next` from a node that another thread may pop, free, or recycle at any moment. Both ABA and the reclamation problem live in those two lines.
- Lock-free because every failed CAS means another thread's CAS succeeded.
- Not wait-free: one thread can lose every race.

subsections.title: 4. The ABA problem
subsections.content:
- CAS compares **values**, not **history**. If the value goes A to B and back to A, CAS cannot tell.
- Classic pop interleaving:
```text
stack: head -> A -> B -> C

T1 (pop):  old = A, next = B          ...preempted...
T2:        pop A, pop B (B freed), push A back      stack: head -> A -> C
T1 resumes: CAS(head, A, B) succeeds  (head == A, as expected)
result:    head -> B  (B is freed memory), and C is reachable only through a dangling node
```
- The CAS check was correct about the head pointer, but `next = B` was computed from a state that no longer exists.
- Where the "same A" comes from in practice:
  - The same node is pushed back (object pools, free lists).
  - The allocator hands the freed address back to a new node (`malloc` very often reuses the most recently freed block of the same size).
- ABA is mostly a problem for **pointer** CAS in structures with removal. A counter that goes 5, 6, 5 has no hidden state, so ABA there is harmless.

subsections.title: 5. Fixing ABA
subsections.content:
| Technique | Idea | Cost / caveat |
|---|---|---|
| **Tagged pointer / version counter** | CAS on `{pointer, counter}`; every successful update bumps the counter, so A with version 5 differs from A with version 7 | needs a double-width CAS (`cmpxchg16b`, often not reported lock-free by GCC, needs `-latomic`), or spare pointer bits (x86-64 user pointers use 48 bits), or a 32-bit index + 32-bit tag in one 64-bit word; tags can wrap |
| **Never reuse memory while referenced** | if A cannot be freed/reused while T1 holds it, A cannot reappear | this is exactly what hazard pointers, epochs and RCU provide, so they fix ABA as a side effect |
| **Reference counting** (`atomic<shared_ptr>`) | a node held by a reader is not destroyed | usually not lock-free; refcount traffic on every access |
| **LL/SC hardware** | store-conditional fails if the location was written at all since the load-linked | not exposed in C++; reservations are fragile; `compare_exchange` stays value-based |
| **Avoid the problem** | bounded preallocated arrays with indices and sequence numbers (ring buffers) | fixed capacity |

- A timer or timestamp is not the standard fix; a monotonically incremented **version/tag counter** is.
- Tag width matters: an 8-bit tag wraps after 256 updates, which a preempted thread can easily sleep through. 32 bits (wrap after ~4 billion updates) is the usual practical choice; 64-bit counters effectively never wrap.

subsections.title: 6. The memory reclamation problem
subsections.content:
- After a successful pop, when is `delete old` safe? Only when **no other thread can still dereference it**. Another thread may have loaded `old` from `head` a moment earlier and be about to read `old->next`.
- `if (p != nullptr)` does not help: `delete` does not null out other threads' copies; a dangling pointer is non-null.
- ABA vs reclamation are **related but different**:
  - ABA: the value came back, CAS cannot see the history (can happen with no `delete` at all, e.g. pooled nodes).
  - Reclamation: a node is freed while someone still holds a pointer to it (use-after-free, even without any ABA).
  - A tagged pointer fixes ABA but **not** use-after-free: the stale `old->next` read can still touch memory returned to the OS. Tags are safe only with type-stable memory (pools that never return memory).
- Reclamation schemes (all: "retire now, free later"):

| Scheme | Reader side | Reclaimer side | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hazard pointers** | publish the pointer you are about to use in a per-thread slot, then **re-validate** it is still reachable | retire to a list; periodically scan all hazard slots, free only unprotected nodes | bounded garbage; a store + full fence per protected access |
| **Epoch-based reclamation (EBR)** | announce "I am in epoch e" when entering an operation, clear when leaving | retired nodes are tagged with the epoch; free when all active threads have moved past it | very cheap reads; one stalled thread blocks **all** reclamation (unbounded garbage) |
| **RCU** (read-copy-update) | read-side critical sections are almost free | writers publish a new version, then wait for a grace period before freeing the old one | ideal for read-mostly data (Linux kernel, config snapshots); writers pay |
| **Reference counting** | increment count before use | free when count reaches 0 | contended refcount on every read; correct lock-free refcounting is subtle |
| **Never free** (type-stable pool) | nothing | nodes go back to a pool, never to the OS | needs tags for ABA; memory never shrinks |

- C++26 standardizes both `std::hazard_pointer` (`<hazard_pointer>`, P2530) and RCU (`<rcu>`, P2545); folly and libcds ship production versions today.
- The reclamation protocol itself must not reintroduce a lock on the read path, otherwise the structure is no longer lock-free.

subsections.title: 7. When lock-free is NOT faster
subsections.content:
- **One hot word:** every push and pop CASes the same `head`. Under contention the cache line ping-pongs and CAS failures waste work. A mutex has the same hot line, and lock-free just spins instead of sleeping.
- **Retry storms:** N threads contending means up to N-1 failed CASes per success; throughput can fall as threads increase. Back-off or elimination arrays help.
- **Uncontended mutex is cheap:** one atomic RMW to lock, one to unlock (futex fast path). A lock-free operation that needs several CASes plus hazard-pointer fences can be slower.
- **Allocation:** `new Node` per push goes through the allocator, which may take a lock and dominates the cost.
- **Reclamation overhead:** hazard pointer publication needs a full fence per access; epoch bookkeeping; retired lists.
- **Complexity cost:** subtle bugs (ABA, use-after-free, memory ordering) that tests rarely reproduce.
- What lock-free **does** buy:
  - No thread can block others by being preempted, page-faulting, or descheduled while holding a lock.
  - No priority inversion, no deadlock, no convoying.
  - Usable from signal handlers and some real-time contexts (if the atomics are lock-free).
  - Often better **tail latency** under oversubscription, even when median throughput is equal or worse.
- Low-latency practice: avoid sharing instead of making sharing lock-free. SPSC ring buffers per producer/consumer pair are wait-free, preallocated, have no ABA and no reclamation problem.

subsections.title: 8. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Lock-free means no mutex in the code." ✅ It is a progress guarantee; a hand-rolled spinlock built from atomics is still **blocking**.
- ❌ "Lock-free means every thread makes progress." ✅ Only the system does; that is wait-free.
- ❌ "A CAS loop is wait-free because nobody waits on a lock." ✅ Unbounded retries make it lock-free only.
- ❌ "Lock-free is automatically faster than a mutex." ✅ Often equal or slower in throughput; the win is progress and tail latency.
- ❌ "Wait-free means lowest latency." ✅ It is a bound on steps, not a speed.
- ❌ "`fetch_add` is always wait-free." ✅ The standard promises no wait-freedom; it is a single `lock xadd` on x86 but an LL/SC retry loop on older ARM; `fetch_or` with a used result is a CAS loop even on x86.
- ❌ "ABA can be fixed with a timer/timestamp." ✅ Use a monotonic version/tag counter (or safe reclamation).
- ❌ "ABA and use-after-free are the same problem." ✅ Related; tags fix ABA, reclamation schemes fix lifetime (and as a side effect ABA).
- ❌ "Check `p != nullptr` before using a popped node." ✅ A dangling pointer is not null.
- ❌ "Just use `shared_ptr` and the problem disappears." ✅ It works for lifetime, but costs atomic refcount traffic and `atomic<shared_ptr>` is usually not lock-free.
- ❌ "Reclamation means threads synchronize with a lock about who deletes." ✅ They coordinate through atomic announcements (hazard slots, epochs) precisely to avoid waiting on each other.

#### 1. Mental model
- "Lock-free" is a **progress guarantee**, not "code without `std::mutex`" and not "fast".
- The test that defines each class: **suspend one thread at the worst possible instruction, forever. Can the others still finish their operations?**
  - Blocking (mutex, spinlock): no, if the suspended thread holds the lock.
  - Lock-free: yes, at least one other thread keeps completing operations.
  - Wait-free: yes, and every running thread finishes within a bounded number of its own steps.
- A lock-free data structure is three problems stacked on top of each other:

| Layer | Question | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| CAS | Is the shared word still what I based my update on? | `compare_exchange` (topic 05) |
| ABA | Did it change away and come back while I was not looking? | tags/version counters, or never reuse memory while it is referenced |
| Memory reclamation | Can another thread still be dereferencing the node I just removed? | hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, RCU, reference counting |

- Writing the CAS loop is the easy 10 percent. ABA and reclamation are where real lock-free code breaks.

#### 2. Progress guarantees

edge_cases.title: A null check does not detect a freed node
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "Before dereferencing `old`, check it is not null."
- What happens: T1 loads `old = A`. T2 pops A and `delete`s it. T1's `old` still holds A's address: `old != nullptr` is true, `old->next` is a use-after-free (UB).
- `delete p` only affects the object, not every copy of the pointer in other threads.
- Fix: a reclamation scheme (hazard pointers, epochs, RCU) or never freeing nodes while the structure is live.

edge_cases.title: A tag counter fixes ABA but not use-after-free
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "With a version counter my pop is safe."
- What happens: pop still reads `old->next` **before** the CAS. If `old` was freed and its page returned to the OS, that read can segfault. The tag only makes the subsequent CAS fail.
- Tags are safe when nodes live in **type-stable memory** (a pool or array that is never released while the structure exists), so the stale read returns garbage that the failing CAS discards.
- Even then, `next` should be an atomic (read `relaxed`) because the stale read can race with the node's new owner writing `next`; a plain field is a formal data race.

edge_cases.title: Your "lock-free" stack calls `new`
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "No mutex in push, so push is lock-free."
- What happens: `new Node` goes to the allocator; glibc `malloc` uses per-thread caches and arenas but can take arena locks and make system calls. The end-to-end operation is only as lock-free as the allocator.
- Low-latency designs preallocate nodes (pools, free lists, ring buffers) so the hot path never allocates.

edge_cases.title: A lock-free algorithm on a non-lock-free atomic
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "I used only `std::atomic`, so the algorithm is lock-free."
- What happens: a double-width tagged pointer `struct { Node* p; uint64_t tag; }` is 16 bytes. With GCC on x86-64, `std::atomic` of it reports `is_always_lock_free == false`, its operations go through `libatomic` (link `-latomic`), and `is_lock_free()` reports `false`.
- The algorithm silently contains locks. Guard with `static_assert(std::atomic<Head>::is_always_lock_free);` and use a 64-bit packed representation (index + tag, or spare pointer bits) when it fails.

edge_cases.title: Tag wraparound
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "Any tag fixes ABA."
- What happens: a preempted thread can sleep through `2^bits` updates. An 8-bit or 16-bit tag (squeezed into spare pointer bits) can wrap back to the same value; CAS then succeeds on a stale `{A, tag}` and ABA returns.
- Make the tag as wide as possible (32 bits in an index+tag word, or a 64-bit counter with DWCAS). Practice task Q6 demonstrates an 8-bit wrap.

edge_cases.title: Epoch-based reclamation and a stalled thread
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "EBR is lock-free, so memory use is bounded."
- What happens: reclamation waits until every active thread has left the old epoch. One thread preempted (or blocked in I/O) inside a read-side section freezes the epoch; retired nodes accumulate without bound.
- Operations stay lock-free, but **memory** is not bounded. Hazard pointers bound unreclaimed nodes to roughly (threads x hazards) plus the scan threshold, at the cost of a fence per protected access.

edge_cases.title: Hazard pointer published without re-validation
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "I stored `old` in my hazard slot, so it is protected."
- What happens: between `old = head.load()` and `hazard.store(old)`, another thread can pop and free `old`; the reclaimer scanned the hazard slots before your store became visible. Protection only counts if, **after** publishing, you re-read `head` and it still equals `old` (so `old` was reachable at a moment when your hazard was already visible).
- The publish and the re-read must not be reordered: use `seq_cst` (or an explicit full fence); see topic 06.

edge_cases.title: A size() on a lock-free container is only a snapshot
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: `if (stack.size() > 0) stack.pop()` is safe, or that an atomic `size_` counter is exact.
- What happens: the size and the head are separate words; between reading one and acting on the other, other threads change both. A separately maintained atomic count can even be temporarily inconsistent with the list.
- Lock-free APIs therefore return status from the operation itself: `std::optional<T> try_pop()`, `bool try_push()`.

code_examples.title: Treiber stack with deferred reclamation
code_examples.explanation:
- A correct lock-free stack for the simple case where popped nodes are only freed when the stack is destroyed (so no ABA and no use-after-free during its life).

- Output: `all values popped exactly once`.
- Push dereferences only its own node. Pop dereferences `old`, which is safe here only because no node is freed or reused until destruction (no address reuse means no ABA).
- `bury` uses a separate `dead_next` link on purpose: a slow thread may still be reading `old->next` of a node that was just popped, and overwriting that field would be a data race.
- Real structures cannot keep every node forever: that is what reclamation schemes solve.

code_examples.title: ABA replayed step by step
code_examples.explanation:
- A deterministic single-threaded replay of the classic interleaving, using the same push/pop as a naive Treiber stack.

- Output:

- The CAS saw `head == A` and succeeded, but installed `B`, a node that T2 already removed and freed. In a real program the `final` walk is a use-after-free.

code_examples.title: Tagged index stack (ABA-safe, 64-bit lock-free CAS)
code_examples.explanation:
- Nodes live in a preallocated pool (type-stable memory); `head` packs a 32-bit node index and a 32-bit version tag into one `uint64_t`, so a plain 8-byte CAS is enough.

- Output:

- Pointer identity is now `{index, version}`; A at version 3 no longer matches A at version 6.
- Works without hazard pointers only because pool memory is never freed while the stack exists.

code_examples.title: Hazard pointers (minimal, one slot per thread)
code_examples.explanation:
- Pop publishes the node it is about to dereference; retired nodes are freed only when no hazard slot holds them.

- Output: `pops=800000 freed during run + at exit = 800000`.
- Steps 1 and 2 are the whole trick: once `old` is announced **and** still the head, any thread that later retires it will see the announcement during `scan` and keep it.
- Hazard pointers also remove ABA here: a protected node cannot be freed and reallocated, so `head == old` really means the same node.
- Cost: a `seq_cst` store (a full barrier on x86) per protected access, plus scanning all slots.

code_examples.title: SPSC ring buffer, wait-free and reclamation-free
code_examples.explanation:
- One producer, one consumer, fixed capacity: each index has a single writer, so no CAS, no ABA, no reclamation. Both operations finish in a bounded number of steps.

- Output: `sum ok`.
- `try_push`/`try_pop` are wait-free; the caller's `while (!try_push)` retry when full is a policy outside the data structure.
- The acquire/release pairs publish the slot contents (topic 06).

code_examples.title: Lock-free is not automatically faster
code_examples.explanation:
- Same push/pop workload on a mutex-protected stack and a Treiber stack. Nodes are preallocated (the allocator is not measured) and each node is pushed exactly once, so no address can come back: no ABA, no reclamation needed.

- Output is machine-dependent. Four runs on a 20-core x86 machine gave about 15 ms (mutex) vs 11 ms (lock-free) with 1 thread, and 310 to 380 ms (mutex) vs 230 to 315 ms (lock-free) with 4 threads: for the same work per thread, both versions got **about 20x slower** with 4 threads, because every operation fights for the one cache line holding `head`. The lock-free version is somewhat faster here, not dramatically, and the ratio changes with core count, CPU and oversubscription.
- With more threads than cores, the mutex version also suffers when a lock holder is preempted; that is where lock-free gains most (progress, tail latency), not in the uncontended case.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between blocking, obstruction-free, lock-free and wait-free algorithms?
interview_qa.answer: Blocking: a delayed thread holding a lock can stop everyone. Obstruction-free: a thread finishes if it runs alone long enough. Lock-free: some thread always finishes in finite steps (system-wide progress). Wait-free: every thread finishes in a bounded number of its own steps.

- Scenario test (how interviewers phrase it):
  - "Threads may starve, but at least one competing thread always completes": **lock-free**.
  - "Every thread completes within a bounded number of its own steps": **wait-free**.
  - "A thread completes if it eventually executes without interference": **obstruction-free**.
- Hierarchy: wait-free > lock-free > obstruction-free > blocking.
- Useful test: freeze any one thread forever at the worst instruction. Blocking algorithms can stall; lock-free ones keep completing operations.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Lock-free means no thread is locked / there is no mutex." The definition is about guaranteed progress, not the absence of a mutex type.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: these are guarantees, not speeds; wait-free often costs more on average (helping schemes, extra metadata). Obstruction-free algorithms can livelock under contention and need back-off or contention managers.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Lock-free: somebody progresses. Wait-free: everybody progresses within a bound.

interview_qa.question: My code uses only std::atomic and no mutex. Is it lock-free?

interview_qa.question: Give the simplest example of a wait-free operation. Is std::atomic<int>::fetch_add always wait-free?

interview_qa.question: Walk me through push and pop of a lock-free (Treiber) stack.
interview_qa.answer: Push: set new->next = head, then CAS head from new->next to new; on failure the CAS refreshes new->next, retry. Pop: load old = head; if null, empty; CAS head from old to old->next; retry on failure. The successful CAS is the linearization point.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Treiber push is easy; pop needs ABA protection and safe reclamation.

interview_qa.question: What is the ABA problem? Walk through a concrete interleaving.
interview_qa.answer: CAS checks only that a value equals what you read, not that it never changed. If it goes A to B and back to A, CAS succeeds although the state your update depended on is gone. In a stack pop, T1 reads head A and next B, sleeps; others pop A, pop B, push A; T1's CAS installs stale B.
interview_qa.explanation:
```text
stack: head -> A -> B -> C
T1: old = A, next = B         (preempted)
T2: pop A, pop B (free B), push A     -> head -> A -> C
T1: CAS(head, A, B) succeeds          -> head -> B (freed), A is lost
```
- The name: the value went A, then B, then A again.
- The bug is not the CAS itself; it is the **cached `next`**, computed from a state that no longer exists.
- Where the recycled A comes from: the same node pushed back (pools/free lists) or `malloc` returning the freed address for a new node.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "CAS guarantees nothing changed since I read it." It guarantees only equality at the moment of the CAS.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: ABA matters when the CAS value **stands for** more state (a pointer with a `next` behind it). For a plain counter, A to B to A is harmless.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CAS compares values, not histories; pointers recycle.

interview_qa.question: How do you fix ABA? Would adding a timestamp work?
interview_qa.answer: Make the CAS word include a version counter that every successful update increments (a tagged pointer), so {A, v5} no longer equals {A, v7}. - Representations:
  - Double-width CAS on `{pointer, 64-bit counter}` (x86-64 `cmpxchg16b`). With GCC this goes through `libatomic`, reports `is_lock_free() == false` and needs `-latomic`.
  - Pack a tag into unused pointer bits (x86-64 user space uses 48 bits; 16 bits free), but a 16-bit tag can wrap.
  - Use a preallocated node array: 32-bit index + 32-bit tag in one `uint64_t` (portable, lock-free 8-byte CAS).
- Timestamps: two updates can share a timestamp, clocks are not monotonic across cores without extra cost, and they still need to be inside the CAS word; a counter is strictly simpler and exact.
- LL/SC hardware detects any intervening write, but C++ exposes only value-based `compare_exchange`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Add a timer or time frame to detect changes." It is the right instinct (extra identity in the CAS) with the wrong mechanism.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: tags fix ABA but not use-after-free; pair them with type-stable memory (a pool never returned to the OS) or a reclamation scheme.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CAS on {pointer, version}; widen the tag enough that it cannot wrap during one preemption.

interview_qa.question: Are the ABA problem and the memory reclamation problem the same thing?
interview_qa.answer: No. ABA is a stale CAS succeeding because a value returned to an old bit pattern; it can happen with no delete at all (pooled nodes). - Tags + freed memory: the stale `old->next` read can still segfault if the page went back to the OS. Tags are only safe with type-stable memory.
- Hazard pointers/EBR prevent a node from being reused while referenced, so the address cannot come back: no ABA either.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "ABA is just use-after-free with a fancy name." They overlap in practice but have different fixes.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in C++ (no garbage collector) reclamation is the harder and more fundamental problem; in Java the GC already prevents reuse while referenced, so ABA on object references is largely a non-issue there.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Version tags answer "did it change?"; reclamation answers "may I free it?".

interview_qa.question: A thread holds a pointer to a node that another thread popped and deleted. Can it protect itself with a null check?
interview_qa.answer: No. delete destroys the object but does not change other copies of the pointer, so the stale pointer is still non-null and dereferencing it is use-after-free (UB). The fix is a reclamation protocol that delays the delete until no thread can hold the pointer.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A non-null pointer can be dangling; only a reclamation scheme makes the dereference safe.

**Explanation:**
```cpp
#include <cstdio>
struct Node { int value; Node* next; };
int main() {
    Node* shared = new Node{1, nullptr};
    Node* mine = shared;          // T1's copy
    delete shared;                // T2 frees it
    shared = nullptr;             // only T2's variable changes
    std::printf("%d\n", mine != nullptr);   // prints 1: the check passes, mine dangles
}
```

interview_qa.question: How do hazard pointers work?
interview_qa.answer: Before dereferencing a shared node, a thread stores its address in a per-thread hazard slot, then re-reads the source to confirm the node is still reachable. Removed nodes are retired to a list; a reclaimer periodically scans all hazard slots and frees only retired nodes no slot mentions.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Reader protocol:
  1. `p = head.load()`
  2. `hazard[me].store(p)` (announce)
  3. if `head.load() != p`, retry (re-validate: p may already have been retired before the announcement was visible)
  4. use `p` safely, then clear the slot.
- Reclaimer: `retire(n)` appends to a local list; when it exceeds a threshold, snapshot all hazard slots and `delete` every retired node not in the snapshot.
- Ordering: the announce store and the re-validating load must not be reordered (store-load), so they need `seq_cst` or a full fence; on x86 that store is an `xchg`/`mfence`.
- Properties: unreclaimed memory bounded by about (threads x slots + threshold); a stalled thread only pins the few nodes it announced.
- C++26 standardizes `std::hazard_pointer` (`<hazard_pointer>`); folly has the reference implementation.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Publish the pointer in the hazard slot and you are protected." Without re-validation the node may already be retired and freed.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: hazard pointers also eliminate ABA for the protected node (it cannot be recycled while announced), and the per-access fence is their main cost compared with epoch schemes.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Announce, re-validate, use; reclaimers skip announced nodes.

interview_qa.question: How does epoch-based reclamation (or RCU) differ from hazard pointers?
interview_qa.answer: Instead of protecting each pointer, a thread announces it is inside an operation in the current epoch. Retired nodes are freed only after every thread has moved past the epoch they were retired in. Reads are cheaper (no per-pointer fence), but one stalled reader blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.
interview_qa.explanation:
- EBR sketch: global epoch `E`; on entry a thread records `local = E` and marks itself active; nodes retired in epoch `e` are freed once all active threads have observed an epoch later than `e` (commonly `e + 2`).
- RCU: readers enter cheap read-side critical sections; a writer copies, modifies, publishes the new version with one pointer store, then waits for a grace period (all pre-existing readers finished) before freeing the old version. Used heavily in the Linux kernel; C++26 adds `<rcu>`.
- Comparison:

| | Hazard pointers | EBR / RCU |
|---|---|---|
| Read-side cost | store + full fence per pointer | near zero per pointer |
| Memory bound | bounded | unbounded if a reader stalls |
| Best for | general structures, bounded memory | read-mostly data, short reads |

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Epoch reclamation is lock-free, so it cannot be held up by a slow thread." Operations stay non-blocking, but **reclamation** waits for the slowest reader.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: trading-system config/reference data (read on every message, updated rarely) is a classic RCU fit; per-message queues usually avoid dynamic nodes entirely.

interview_qa.question: Why not just use std::shared_ptr (or std::atomic<std::shared_ptr>) for nodes in a lock-free stack?
interview_qa.answer: It does solve lifetime (a node is not destroyed while someone holds a reference, so no use-after-free or ABA), but every access does atomic refcount updates on shared cache lines, atomic<shared_ptr> is usually implemented with an internal lock (not lock-free), and destroying a long chain can recurse deeply.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<Node>> head;` makes `head.load()` return an owning reference; `old->next` is safe to read.

  - Refcount increment and decrement per load: contended RMW on the control block.
  - libstdc++ and MSVC implement `atomic<shared_ptr>` with a lock bit or spin lock: `is_lock_free()` is false, so the "lock-free" stack is not lock-free.
  - Releasing the last reference to a long list destroys nodes recursively (`next` destructor chain), which can overflow the stack.
- Fine for low-rate, correctness-first code; rarely used on hot paths.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`shared_ptr` is thread-safe, so the problem disappears for free." Only the count is thread-safe, and it is not free.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: designing lock-free reference counting correctly (split counts, differential counting) is itself an advanced problem; production code uses hazard pointers or epochs instead.

interview_qa.question: Is a lock-free data structure faster than a mutex-protected one?
interview_qa.answer: Not necessarily. Both serialize on the same hot cache line, lock-free adds failed-CAS retries and reclamation overhead, and an uncontended mutex is just two atomic RMWs. Lock-free wins on progress (no stalling behind a preempted holder) and often tail latency, not raw throughput.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured (4 threads, push/pop on one stack): both versions about 20x slower than single-threaded; lock-free modestly faster, not dramatically.
- Where lock-free loses or ties:
  - high contention on one word (retry storms),
  - per-node allocation (`new` may lock) and reclamation fences,
  - more CASes per operation than a mutex's lock + unlock.
- Where it wins:
  - oversubscription: a mutex holder preempted mid-critical-section stalls everyone,

interview_qa.question: Your lock-free push does `new Node(v)` every time. Is the push still lock-free?
interview_qa.answer: The CAS algorithm is, but the operation as a whole is only as non-blocking as the allocator. General-purpose malloc can take arena locks and make system calls, so end to end it is not guaranteed lock-free and its latency is unpredictable. Low-latency code preallocates nodes or uses fixed-size pools.
interview_qa.explanation:
- glibc malloc: fast per-thread cache (tcache) path without locks, but arena locks and `mmap`/`brk` on slow paths.
- Page faults on first touch of new memory are another hidden stall.

  - Preallocated node pool with a lock-free free list (which itself needs ABA protection, e.g. tagged indices).
  - Bounded ring buffers (no per-element allocation at all).

interview_qa.question: Why are SPSC ring buffers so popular in low-latency systems compared with general lock-free queues?
interview_qa.answer: With one producer and one consumer each index has exactly one writer, so no CAS is needed: push and pop are a few loads and stores with acquire/release, wait-free and bounded. Slots are preallocated, so there is no allocation, no ABA and no reclamation problem.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Producer owns `tail`, consumer owns `head`; each reads the other's index with acquire and publishes its own with release (topic 06).
- Power-of-two capacity and masking for cheap wraparound; `alignas(64)` on the two indices to avoid false sharing.
- Multi-producer/multi-consumer queues need CAS to reserve slots, and **reservation is not publication**: a producer can reserve slot 10, stall, while slot 11 is already published; per-slot sequence numbers solve that.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Any lock-free queue is equally good." MPMC designs carry CAS contention, per-slot state and much more complexity.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: structure the system as a pipeline of SPSC links (one queue per producer/consumer pair) to keep every hop wait-free.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Avoid the hard problems (CAS, ABA, reclamation) by giving each index a single writer.

interview_qa.question: Why does LL/SC hardware avoid ABA, and why doesn't C++ simply use it?
interview_qa.answer: Store-conditional fails if the location was written at all since the load-linked, even if the value returned to A: it detects writes, not values. But reservations are fragile and x86 lacks LL/SC, so C++ exposes only value-based compare_exchange.
interview_qa.explanation:
- ARM (`ldxr`/`stxr`), POWER (`lwarx`/`stwcx.`), RISC-V (`lr`/`sc`) provide LL/SC; x86 has only value-based `cmpxchg`.
- In theory an LL/SC pop (`LL head; read next; SC head = next`) is ABA-immune. In practice the `next` load between LL and SC may break the reservation, and architectures restrict what can happen inside the window.
- `compare_exchange_weak`'s permission to fail spuriously exists to allow this mapping efficiently.
- C++ code must be portable to x86, so it cannot rely on LL/SC semantics: use tags or reclamation.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Spurious failure of `weak` protects against ABA." No: `compare_exchange` is value-based on every platform; a value that returned to A still matches.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: newer ARM (LSE, ARMv8.1) adds value-based `cas` and `ldadd` instructions that compilers use when targeting it (GCC also picks them at runtime via outline atomics), so modern ARM C++ code gets pure value semantics too.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: LL/SC detects writes, CAS detects values; C++ gives you values, so you handle ABA yourself.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
40000 40000 40000
inc_a: blocking. inc_b: lock-free (not wait-free). inc_c: wait-free on x86-64 (single lock xadd), but the C++ standard does not guarantee it.
```

**Explanation:**
- All three are correct, so the output is the same; they differ in **progress guarantee**, not in result.
- `inc_a`: if the thread holding `m` is preempted, every other caller waits. Blocking.
- `inc_b`: a failed CAS means another thread's CAS succeeded (system-wide progress), but one thread can lose indefinitely. Lock-free.
- `inc_c`: compiles to `lock xadd`, no retry loop: each call completes in bounded steps. On LL/SC CPUs without LSE it becomes a retry loop (lock-free only).
- **Key Concept:** Progress guarantees classify how threads can stall each other, not correctness or speed.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.answer: Bug: the CAS result is ignored. Prints a run-dependent count below 400000 (pushes that lost the race, or failed spuriously, are silently dropped).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `compare_exchange_weak` fails whenever another thread changed `head` in between (and may also fail spuriously). Without a loop, the push simply does not happen.
- No data race: the node is still private when the CAS fails; it just never gets linked.
- Even a single-threaded program could lose pushes on LL/SC hardware because of spurious failure.
- **Key Concept:** A CAS that can fail must be in a retry loop (or its failure must be handled).

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer: Not correct. Prints a run-dependent count below 400000: nodes pushed by other threads during a retry become unreachable.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- After a failed CAS, `old` is refreshed with the current head, but `n->next` still points to the **original** head.
- The retry then succeeds with `head = n` while `n->next` skips every node pushed in between. Those nodes are cut out of the list.
- No data race and no crash: the list is silently missing nodes. Only a count check reveals it.
- The idiomatic form passes `n->next` itself as the `expected` argument, so the CAS refreshes the link directly.
- **Key Concept:** Everything derived from `expected` must be recomputed on each retry.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
T1 CAS: success
stack: B(removed) C(removed) D
```

**Explanation:**
- T1 read `head == A` and `next == B`.
- T2 popped A, B, C and pushed A back, so `head == A` again, now with `A->next == D`.
- T1's CAS compares only the pointer: `A == A`, so it succeeds and installs the stale `B`.
- The stack now starts with B and C, which T2 owns (and may already have freed), and A is lost. That is the **ABA problem**: the value went A, B (other states), A.
- In real code with `delete`, walking this list is a use-after-free.
- **Key Concept:** CAS proves the value is equal now, not that nothing changed; the cached `next` is the casualty.
